title: Navigating the CMS TEAM Mandate: A Hospital Leader’s Webinar Guide
text:
A well-done surgery is a good starting point — but it’s not a guarantee. TEAM holds us accountable for everything that follows.

The OR door is no longer the finish line. For most surgeons, clinical accountability has historically ended at the operation or the post-op visit. The CMS TEAM model extends that accountability across the full 30-day post-discharge window — and the comorbidities that drive complications are now part of the surgeon’s performance record.
An opportunity, not just a penalty. For a high-volume orthopedic surgeon performing 300–700 joint replacements per year, TEAM creates a mechanism to standardize excellent care across the entire community — and to be measured and rewarded for it.
Data over reputation. Real-time episode data — not just outcome scores — shows which surgeons are actually delivering on cost and quality. That becomes the performance standard going forward.
Not one-size-fits-all. Roughly 20% of any TEAM implementation is specific to local environment: community resources, referral patterns, and post-acute infrastructure differ significantly between a large California health system and a rural Oklahoma hospital.
Shared accountability, finally. TEAM unites the CPT-code world that physicians live in with the DRG world that hospitals operate in. It creates a shared financial stake that previous value-based care models rarely achieved.

title: Navigating the CMS TEAM Mandate: A Hospital Leader’s Webinar Guide
text:
The CMS TEAM model (Transforming Episode Accountability Model) is a mandatory Medicare bundled-payment program administered by the CMS Innovation Center. It launched January 1, 2026 and runs through December 31, 2030. It holds hospitals accountable for the cost and quality of five surgical episodes, including all Medicare Part A and B spending from the anchor procedure through 30 days post-discharge.



721 acute-care hospitals across 188 core-based statistical areas are mandated to participate in the CMS TEAM model. Participation is not voluntary — CMS selected the hospitals.



Five procedures: lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR), surgical hip and femur fracture treatment (SHFFT), spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), and major bowel procedure.



From the date of discharge following the anchor surgical procedure, all Medicare Part A and Part B spending for 30 days is included in the episode — readmissions, emergency department visits, post-acute care, skilled nursing, and home health, among other services. Medicare Advantage spending is excluded.



Track 1 is the Year 1 entry track — upside-only with no downside risk, capped at 10%. Track 2 applies to safety-net and rural hospitals in Years 2–5, with both upside and downside capped at 10%. Track 3 is full two-sided risk at 20% stop-gain and stop-loss; it applies to all non-safety-net, non-rural hospitals from Year 2 onward and qualifies as an Advanced APM under MIPS.



Up to 20% of Medicare reimbursement from the five covered surgical episodes is at stake under Track 3. Depending on a hospital’s volume and historical performance, that can represent tens of millions of dollars annually. Rainfall’s analysis of a California health system identified $73.4 million in potential upside across five years.



No. The CMS TEAM model is mandatory for the 721 hospitals CMS selected. There is no opt-out provision and no voluntary on-ramp alternative.



CJR-X covered only lower extremity joint replacement and was a voluntary program. CMS TEAM covers five surgical procedures, is mandatory, runs five years with automatic risk escalation, and reaches a 20% upside/downside cap under Track 3 — significantly larger stakes and broader scope than CJR-X.



Under CMS TEAM, value-based care means the hospital’s Medicare reimbursement is tied to the quality and cost of the entire surgical episode — not just the inpatient stay. Hospitals that reduce unnecessary post-acute spending, prevent readmissions, and hit quality benchmarks receive incentive payments. Those that underperform face financial penalties.

Hospitals that fail to manage episode costs and quality metrics face annual penalty payments up to 20% of covered episode reimbursement. For high-volume surgical programs, that exposure can reach $8 million or more per year. Additionally, unmanaged episodes under Track 3 carry both upside forfeiture and active financial penalties.

title: CMS TEAM by Procedure: 204,000 Episodes, Five Surgeries
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          CMS TEAM Episode Volume Bundled Payments Data Analysis sandbox-blog
        
        Media
        
        A data-first breakdown of the 2023 Medicare episode volume across all five CMS TEAM procedure types — what the numbers mean for mandated hospitals going into 2027.

        
          
             Jennifer Tim-Diamond
          
          ·
          July 22, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



Over 200k TEAM episodes in 2023
Orthopedics dominate volume
Lower-volume CABG carries high cost
Volume shapes risk exposure



Five surgical procedures. 721 mandated hospitals. One number that ties them together: 204,014 — the total Medicare fee-for-service episodes recorded at CMS TEAM-participating hospitals in 2023, the final full year before the model went live.
That figure comes from the Institute for Accountable Care and the American College of Surgeons, which analyzed CMS claims data from the 188 selected Core-Based Statistical Areas to model what the TEAM mandate would actually look like at scale. The short answer: it is not evenly distributed.
<BlogChartFigure src={“/charts/team-episode-volume.png”} alt={“Bar chart showing 2023 CMS TEAM episode volume by procedure type”} caption={“LEJR accounts for 118,155 episodes — 58% of total TEAM volume. CABG represents only 5% but carries the highest per-episode cost at $52,934.”} source={“Institute for Accountable Care / ACS analysis of CMS IPPS FY2025 claims data. Rainfall Health.”} />


Lower extremity joint replacement — hip and knee arthroplasty — accounts for 118,155 cases, or 58% of all TEAM episodes. For most mandated hospitals, TEAM is, operationally, a hip and knee program. The other four procedures matter financially, but LEJR is where volume concentrates and where the majority of reconciliation outcomes will be determined.
That concentration has a direct implication for preparation strategy. Hospitals that have strong post-acute discharge protocols for joint replacement patients — coordinated SNF partnerships, home health networks, surgeon-aligned care pathways — are better positioned under TEAM than those that have historically treated LEJR as a high-volume, routine service requiring minimal post-discharge coordination.



Spinal fusion ranks second at 30,689 cases (15% of total). The procedure carries an average baseline episode cost of $51,237 — more than twice LEJR’s average of $24,540. That means a spinal fusion episode that runs above the CMS target price generates a larger dollar penalty per case than an equivalent LEJR miss.
SHFFT (surgical hip and femur fracture treatment) represents 12% of volume at 25,427 cases. These are largely unplanned admissions — a patient with a fall-related fracture, not an elective procedure — which makes the 30-day episode window significantly harder to manage. Post-discharge spending runs 63% of the total average episode cost of $46,615, the highest post-discharge ratio of the five procedure types.



Major bowel procedures — colorectal resections and related surgeries — account for 19,723 cases (10%). The patient mix is heterogeneous, ranging from elective colorectal surgery to emergency bowel resections. That variability makes benchmarking harder. CMS applies a 1.5% discount factor to major bowel target prices (vs. 2.0% for LEJR), a concession to the complexity of the patient population.
<BlogChartFigure src={“/charts/team-post-discharge-share.png”} alt={“Stacked bar chart showing post-discharge spending share by procedure”} caption={“SHFFT episodes have the highest post-discharge cost ratio at 63% — those are fracture patients whose rehabilitation needs extend far beyond the hospital walls. LEJR post-discharge spending averages 40% of the total episode cost.”} source={“CMS IPPS FY2025 Final Rule preamble (89 FR 68986), Table X.A.3.a. Rainfall Health.”} />



Coronary artery bypass graft surgery represents only 5% of TEAM episodes at 10,020 cases, but it carries the highest average episode cost at $52,934. The post-discharge cost share for CABG (22%) is lower than SHFFT or LEJR — the acute hospitalization itself drives most of the episode cost. But when CABG episodes exceed the CMS target price, the average loss is $15,142 per episode, the largest average loss of the five procedure types.
Hospitals with CABG programs should note that their total TEAM exposure per over-target episode is roughly 6× higher than LEJR. Even a small number of high-cost CABG episodes can meaningfully shift annual reconciliation outcomes.



Performance Year 1 (2026) carries no downside financial risk — hospitals can only gain. PY2 and beyond introduce two-sided risk for most participants, with stop-loss limits of up to 20% of the target price. The 2023 episode volume data tells hospitals exactly where that risk will concentrate.
For a typical 400-bed mandated hospital with 350 LEJR episodes, 80 spinal fusions, 60 SHFFT cases, 50 bowel procedures, and 20 CABG procedures annually, the TEAM reconciliation will be dominated by LEJR outcomes — but a single bad quarter on CABG can offset months of LEJR gains.



The 2023 episode volume figures in this analysis are drawn from the Institute for Accountable Care and American College of Surgeons (ACS) analysis of CMS claims data for the 188 TEAM-selected Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs), published in conjunction with ACS advocacy materials on the TEAM Final Rule (FY2025 IPPS, 89 FR 68986). CMS identified episodes using Medicare Standard Analytic Files (SAFs) — claims-based administrative data, not clinical registries — with MS-DRG and ICD-10-PCS procedure codes to attribute each episode to one of the five TEAM procedure categories.
A critical methodological note: these counts reflect 2023 claims data — the most recent year for which complete episode-level analysis is publicly available prior to the January 1, 2026 TEAM start date. Actual 2026 episode volumes will differ for several reasons: post-acute care utilization patterns have been shifting toward ambulatory surgery center (ASC) settings for LEJR in particular, which may reduce inpatient episode attributions; coding practices evolve with ICD-10-PCS updates; and some hospitals in the 741-hospital September 2024 list subsequently closed, merged, or changed IPPS payment status, reducing the March 2026 active participant count to 721.
For planning purposes, the 2023 data provides the most granular public benchmark available. Individual hospital TEAM target price files — distributed through the CMS Innovation Center participant portal after executing a Data Sharing Agreement — contain hospital-specific historical episode counts and costs that supersede these national estimates for financial modeling.
(Source: American College of Surgeons. (2024). TEAM episode volume analysis. ACS advocacy materials.) (Source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (2024). FY2025 IPPS Final Rule, 89 FR 68986.)



The concentration of 58% of TEAM volume in a single procedure type (LEJR) has a policy implication that extends beyond financial modeling. It means that TEAM is, in practical operational terms, primarily a joint replacement accountability program with four ancillary episode types. Hospital leaders who treat TEAM as a comprehensive surgical quality initiative will build very different infrastructure than those who correctly identify it as primarily a hip-and-knee episode management challenge.
The Finkelstein et al. (2018) JAMA analysis of mandatory LEJR bundled payments found that discharge to institutional post-acute care fell 3.6 percentage points — an 11.4% relative reduction — in CBSAs where the bundled payment was mandatory, with no statistically significant change in patient outcomes. This finding suggests that a meaningful share of current LEJR SNF placements are clinically substitutable with home health, and that the financial incentive of TEAM will accelerate what clinical judgment alone has not.
For the four remaining procedure types — spinal fusion (15%), SHFFT (12%), major bowel (10%), and CABG (5%) — the volume concentration is lower but the per-episode financial stakes are higher. A hospital that optimizes LEJR episode management without addressing CABG may miss the highest-leverage individual episode improvement opportunity in its portfolio. Strategic TEAM preparation requires a procedure-type-specific analysis, not a single aggregate approach.
(Source: Finkelstein, A., Ji, Y., Mahoney, N., & Skinner, J. S. (2018). JAMA, 320(9), 892–900.)





204,014 Medicare FFS episodes were recorded at TEAM-mandated hospitals in 2023, according to the Institute for Accountable Care / ACS analysis of IPPS FY2025 data.



LEJR (lower extremity joint replacement — hip and knee) accounts for 58% of all TEAM episodes — 118,155 cases in 2023.



CABG (coronary artery bypass graft) has the highest average episode cost at $52,934, based on 2021 baseline data from the CMS IPPS FY2025 Final Rule.



SHFFT (surgical hip and femur fracture treatment) averages 63% of its $46,615 episode cost in the post-discharge period — the highest of the five procedures. These are largely unplanned admissions (fall injuries) with complex post-acute needs.

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          sandbox-news
        
        Media
        
        A briefing on CMS TEAM, CJR-X, and the companies chasing them.

        
          
             Rainfall Research
          
          ·
          July 08, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



Innovaccer pushes TEAM software
Optum flags coding risk
Milliman adds actuarial tooling
CJR-X proposal expands joint episodes





Innovaccer, a health-tech firm, launched Atlas, a “population health operating system,” on January 22nd. The product extends the firm’s outcomes-tracking software beyond value-based contracts into fee-for-service arrangements, suggesting the company sees its future well beyond compliance work for any single CMS model.
It follows a sustained push into the bundled-payments space: a guide for hospital executives on navigating TEAM, a webinar, a YouTube explainer, and a two-day conference for health systems this spring. Oracle, a software giant, recently named Innovaccer a competitor of its own health-data ambitions — no small compliment.
(Source: Innovaccer, “Gearing Up for CMS TEAM: A Guide for Healthcare Leaders,” March 18, 2025.) (Source: Innovaccer, “Innovaccer Launches Atlas: The Population Health Operating System to Deliver Outcomes Beyond Value-Based Care,” press release, January 22, 2026.)



Optum Advisory, a consulting arm of UnitedHealth Group, published an analysis in November finding that most hospitals mandated into TEAM will face financial exposure once downside risk begins in 2027.
The firm’s sharper finding concerned coding, not payment policy: one facility it studied had left roughly two-thirds of its episodes without the diagnosis codes needed to secure favorable risk adjustment. For Optum, whose business model favors advisory fees over software subscriptions, this is a sales pitch as much as a research finding.
(Source: Advisory.com (Optum), “What hospitals need to know about TEAM for 2026,” November 25, 2025.) (Source: Optum, Cleveland Clinic bundled payment case study.)



Milliman, an actuarial firm, is making its own case through data rather than diagnosis. Its MedInsight Bundles product, promoted in a November write-up, offers hospitals episode-level profitability tracking and settlement auditing for TEAM.
A January outlook named TEAM and the newer Ambulatory Surgical Model among the top issues facing health systems this year, and a February note extended Milliman’s pitch to skilled-nursing facilities eyeing partnerships with hospitals under the model.
(Source: Milliman/MedInsight, “Turning CMS’s TEAM Model into a competitive advantage,” November 26, 2025.) (Source: Milliman, “6 issues Milliman is watching for health systems and provider organizations in 2026,” January 8, 2026.) (Source: Milliman, “The CMS Transforming Episode Accountability Model: 4 reasons why it’s an opportunity for skilled nursing facilities…,” February 5, 2026.)



CMS, the federal agency that runs Medicare, proposed on April 10th a new mandatory bundled-payment model, CJR-X, that would eventually cover more than 2,500 hospitals nationwide — more than three times the number mandated into TEAM.
If finalized, it would take effect on October 1st, 2027, and apply nationwide to joint-replacement episodes, a marked departure from TEAM’s regional pilot design. None of the three companies above have yet said a public word about it.
(Source: CMS, FY2027 Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) Proposed Rule (CJR-X), April 10, 2026.) (Source: Forvis Mazars, “CJR-X: Unpacking CMS’ New Mandatory Bundled Payment Model,” May 2026.) (Source: Bass, Berry & Sims, “CMS Proposes Nationwide Mandatory Bundled Payment Model for Joint Replacements,” April 2026.) (Source: Lexology, “CMS Proposes Resurrection and Nationwide Expansion of Mandatory Joint Replacement Bundled Payment Model (CJR-X),” April 2026.)



TEAM itself enters a quieter phase. The model’s first year carries no downside financial risk, giving hospitals what one analyst called a “dress rehearsal.” That grace period ends in 2027, when penalties of up to a fifth of a hospital’s target reimbursement come into force — precisely the moment CJR-X is due to arrive alongside it.
(Source: CMS, “TEAM (Transforming Episode Accountability Model),” model page.) (Source: HFMA, “Hospitals can use 2026 to prepare for CMS TEAM bundled payment risk,” March 7, 2026.) (Source: ACS Bulletin, “New TEAM Payment Model Brings Opportunities, Challenges for Surgeons and Hospitals,” January 2025.)

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
Innovaccer, a health-tech firm, launched Atlas, a “population health operating system,” on January 22nd. The product extends the firm’s outcomes-tracking software beyond value-based contracts into fee-for-service arrangements, suggesting the company sees its future well beyond compliance work for any single CMS model.
It follows a sustained push into the bundled-payments space: a guide for hospital executives on navigating TEAM, a webinar, a YouTube explainer, and a two-day conference for health systems this spring. Oracle, a software giant, recently named Innovaccer a competitor of its own health-data ambitions — no small compliment.
(Source: Innovaccer, “Gearing Up for CMS TEAM: A Guide for Healthcare Leaders,” March 18, 2025.) (Source: Innovaccer, “Innovaccer Launches Atlas: The Population Health Operating System to Deliver Outcomes Beyond Value-Based Care,” press release, January 22, 2026.)

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
Optum Advisory, a consulting arm of UnitedHealth Group, published an analysis in November finding that most hospitals mandated into TEAM will face financial exposure once downside risk begins in 2027.
The firm’s sharper finding concerned coding, not payment policy: one facility it studied had left roughly two-thirds of its episodes without the diagnosis codes needed to secure favorable risk adjustment. For Optum, whose business model favors advisory fees over software subscriptions, this is a sales pitch as much as a research finding.
(Source: Advisory.com (Optum), “What hospitals need to know about TEAM for 2026,” November 25, 2025.) (Source: Optum, Cleveland Clinic bundled payment case study.)

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
Milliman, an actuarial firm, is making its own case through data rather than diagnosis. Its MedInsight Bundles product, promoted in a November write-up, offers hospitals episode-level profitability tracking and settlement auditing for TEAM.
A January outlook named TEAM and the newer Ambulatory Surgical Model among the top issues facing health systems this year, and a February note extended Milliman’s pitch to skilled-nursing facilities eyeing partnerships with hospitals under the model.
(Source: Milliman/MedInsight, “Turning CMS’s TEAM Model into a competitive advantage,” November 26, 2025.) (Source: Milliman, “6 issues Milliman is watching for health systems and provider organizations in 2026,” January 8, 2026.) (Source: Milliman, “The CMS Transforming Episode Accountability Model: 4 reasons why it’s an opportunity for skilled nursing facilities…,” February 5, 2026.)

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
CMS, the federal agency that runs Medicare, proposed on April 10th a new mandatory bundled-payment model, CJR-X, that would eventually cover more than 2,500 hospitals nationwide — more than three times the number mandated into TEAM.
If finalized, it would take effect on October 1st, 2027, and apply nationwide to joint-replacement episodes, a marked departure from TEAM’s regional pilot design. None of the three companies above have yet said a public word about it.
(Source: CMS, FY2027 Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) Proposed Rule (CJR-X), April 10, 2026.) (Source: Forvis Mazars, “CJR-X: Unpacking CMS’ New Mandatory Bundled Payment Model,” May 2026.) (Source: Bass, Berry & Sims, “CMS Proposes Nationwide Mandatory Bundled Payment Model for Joint Replacements,” April 2026.) (Source: Lexology, “CMS Proposes Resurrection and Nationwide Expansion of Mandatory Joint Replacement Bundled Payment Model (CJR-X),” April 2026.)

title: The Week in Bundled Payments
text:
TEAM itself enters a quieter phase. The model’s first year carries no downside financial risk, giving hospitals what one analyst called a “dress rehearsal.” That grace period ends in 2027, when penalties of up to a fifth of a hospital’s target reimbursement come into force — precisely the moment CJR-X is due to arrive alongside it.
(Source: CMS, “TEAM (Transforming Episode Accountability Model),” model page.) (Source: HFMA, “Hospitals can use 2026 to prepare for CMS TEAM bundled payment risk,” March 7, 2026.) (Source: ACS Bulletin, “New TEAM Payment Model Brings Opportunities, Challenges for Surgeons and Hospitals,” January 2025.)

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
To outside observers, a data governance role sounds like an endless cycle of policy memos and regulatory compliance checklists. In practice, Han describes the role as fundamentally operational.
Every morning begins with a concrete problem that someone wants health data to solve:

Operations: Enabling hospital operations teams to track bed availability, surgical throughput, and staffing ratios across five distinct medical campuses.
Population Health: Helping clinical quality leaders identify patients with chronic diseases who are due for preventive screenings before acute complications develop.
Efficiency: Streamlining administrative workflows so physicians and nurses spend less time charting and more time with patients.
Translating Research to Bedside: Creating secure, compliant data enclaves where academic researchers and clinicians can collaborate to develop new therapeutics, validate algorithms, and test novel care pathways.

In every case, the technical capability to move the data is rarely the hardest part. The challenge is ensuring that data use serves a verified institutional need, complies with federal and state privacy statutes, and preserves patient confidence.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
One of the most persistent refrains among health technology founders and clinical innovators is that legal and compliance teams are “where good ideas go to die.”
Han rejects that framing outright:

Lawyers don’t slow projects down. Late lawyers do.
— Cora Han

The breakdown occurs when a clinical or operational team spends nine to twelve months evaluating a software vendor, refining a pilot scope, and configuring dashboards, only to hand the completed vendor agreement to legal two weeks before the targeted go-live date.
At that late stage, in-house counsel uncovers fundamental structural flaws:

Overbroad data rights that run afoul of HIPAA or state privacy statutes (such as California’s CMIA).
Inadequate cybersecurity protocols or undisclosed downstream sub-processors.
Ambiguous data retention, re-identification, or secondary model-training clauses.
Workflow assumptions that create regulatory or clinical liability under Medicare programs.

When legal raises these critical flags, the project grinds to a halt. The operational champions blame legal for obstruction. In reality, the initiative stalled because governance was treated as an afterthought rather than a primary architecture requirement.


To avoid the late-lawyer trap, health systems must establish a structured, multidisciplinary table from day one:

Dedicated Governance Forums: Convening clinical champions, IT security engineers, and legal counsel on a recurring schedule so evaluations do not stall in scheduling purgatory.
A Shared Vocabulary: Clinicians, data scientists, and attorneys must learn enough of each other’s domain to communicate without suspicion. Compliance concerns must be specific and grounded, not used as a generic veto.
A Single Problem Statement: Defining precisely what clinical friction is being resolved, why existing systems cannot solve it, and what minimal data set is required.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
Under CMS’s mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (CMS TEAM), 721 hospitals are held financially accountable for total Medicare Part A and B spending across a 30-day post-discharge window following five major inpatient surgical episodes:

Lower-extremity joint replacement (LEJR)
Surgical hip and femur fracture treatment (SHFFT)
Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)
Major bowel procedures
Spinal fusion

Because the majority of complications, readmissions, and spending occur after the patient leaves the acute care hospital — in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs), inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and home health agencies — TEAM is, in practice, a distributed care coordination and data-sharing mandate.
When asked why data does not flow smoothly across this continuum, Han chooses a precise word: uneven.










Care Continuum Setting
Technology Infrastructure
Dedicated Resources
Primary Operational Focus




Acute Care Hospitals
Enterprise EHR (Epic/Cerner), real-time HL7/FHIR feeds, automated clinical alert systems
In-house legal counsel, data security engineers, clinical informaticists
Acute stabilization, surgical intervention, throughput, bed capacity


Skilled Nursing (SNFs)
Fragmented point-of-care EHRs, manual portal data entry, legacy software
Lean administrative teams, high nursing turnover, outsourced IT
Functional rehabilitation, ADL recovery, medication administration


Community Organizations
Paper charts, spreadsheets, unscheduled phone calls, secure faxes
Social workers, patient navigators, family caregivers, case managers
Social drivers of health (SDOH), housing, nutrition, transportation




The friction across this care continuum does not stem from a lack of goodwill. Surgeons, hospital case managers, SNF directors of nursing, and home health coordinators all want the patient to heal without complication. The breakdown stems from four structural disparities:

Storage Disparities: Legacy EHR platforms that do not speak the same clinical dialects or format transition summaries consistently.
Process Fragmentation: Incompatible handoff timelines, referral documentation standards, and medication reconciliation workflows.
Resource Asymmetry: Large medical systems possess multi-million-dollar health informatics teams; post-acute facilities often rely on single-person contracted IT support.
Data Capture Variance: The acute-care chart captures surgical minutiae; the post-acute facility needs functional mobility, wound status, and social support availability.

As Eddie Qureshi emphasized during the discussion, health policy cannot assume an idealized world where every nursing home runs the same infrastructure as an academic medical center. Technology must meet providers where they operate today.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
For more than two decades, the healthcare industry has treated interoperability as a plumbing problem: deploy FHIR APIs, connect to regional health information exchanges (HIEs), establish Direct secure messaging protocols, and data will flow.
Yet data sharing across acute and post-acute care remains persistently fragmented. Why?

Asked for the biggest challenge, she offers one broad word: There is a trust gap. It’s not the pipes. It’s the trust.
— Cora Han

Han dissects this trust gap across two operational planes:


Hospitals and post-acute facilities are frequently competitors in certain outpatient service lines while being forced collaborators under bundled payment models. When a hospital requests direct access to a post-acute partner’s clinical records, immediate questions arise:

Will you use our clinical documentation to evaluate, penalize, or deselect our facility from your preferred network?
How will the data be transmitted, and who assumes financial liability if a breach occurs?
Who is legally liable if a missed notification or incomplete transfer leads to an adverse patient event?

Without bounded, pre-negotiated legal frameworks, providers default to defensive data withholding.



Patients are acutely aware of the commercialization of personal information. If patients fear their surgical details, biometric readings, or health status will be shared with data brokers, commercial insurers, or advertisers, they withhold sensitive details from their doctors.
True interoperability unlocks only when both planes are resolved: institutions agree on purpose-bound operational scopes, and patients know their information is guarded by enforceable institutional commitments.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
For technology companies seeking to partner with health systems, Han shares three core principles that accelerate enterprise adoption far more effectively than a slide deck of software features:


Health systems do not have the operational capacity or clinician goodwill to mandate yet another standalone login portal. Technology that forces doctors or care managers to toggle between windows will be ignored. Software must integrate natively into established daily workflows.



Proprietary “black-box” algorithms will not pass clinical governance committees. Vendors must be capable of demonstrating to medical directors and ethics boards why a model generates specific recommendations, what validation datasets were used, and how algorithmic bias was measured and mitigated.



Nothing stalls health system procurement faster than a half-filled security questionnaire or vague answers regarding sub-processors. Vendors that arrive with standardized, pre-packaged SOC2 Type II reports, penetration testing summaries, and architectural diagrams build immediate trust.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
As the conversation concluded, Eddie Qureshi and Cora Han turned to the long-term trajectory of artificial intelligence across American healthcare.
When the automobile first appeared, early observers described it as a “horseless carriage.” The metric of success was straightforward: does it pull a carriage slightly faster or cheaper than a horse? Only years later did society recognize that automobiles fundamentally transformed urban planning, commerce, supply chains, and public health.
Healthcare is currently navigating its “fast horse” era of AI. Systems are deploying tools to draft patient portal replies slightly faster, summarize visit notes a few minutes quicker, or automate routine scheduling calls.

Don’t stop at making existing things go faster. Ask how technology might change the way care is provided. It is really kind of our duty to think in the big picture about what the large-scale potential could be.
— Cora Han

When true care-continuum infrastructure is established — connecting acute hospitals, post-acute facilities, and community health workers through shared governance and accountability — healthcare will stop trying to make fragmented, analog processes run faster. It will finally deliver the continuous, proactive care transitions that patients deserve.

title: The Trust Gap: Cora Han on Health Data Governance, Responsible AI, and Care Transitions
text:
A Chief Health Data Officer (CHDO) oversees health data governance, security, and utilization strategy. At institutions like UC Health, the CHDO bridges clinical operations, IT engineering, research data enclaves, and legal compliance to ensure patient data is used effectively to improve clinical outcomes while safeguarding privacy and institutional trust.



Care transitions between hospitals and SNFs typically break down due to structural disparities in health IT infrastructure, incompatible workflow handoffs, and a lack of pre-negotiated trust agreements. While both parties want the patient to heal, defensive data withholding and fragmented EHR systems prevent clinical teams from accessing actionable patient information in real time.



Under CMS TEAM, hospitals are held financially accountable for all Medicare Part A and B spending across a 30-day post-discharge window. Because post-acute providers deliver the majority of care during this period, hospitals must establish secure, compliant, and purpose-bound data agreements to track patient progress, prevent complications, and avoid readmission penalties without violating HIPAA.



As Cora Han explains, “Lawyers don’t slow projects down. Late lawyers do.” When operational or clinical teams negotiate software contracts for months before bringing in legal counsel, lawyers are forced to halt deployments to resolve critical privacy, cybersecurity, and secondary data-use vulnerabilities that should have been addressed during initial scoping.



CIOs and clinical executives should evaluate eight fundamental governance domains: clinical necessity, comparative clinical efficacy, data minimization, data retention policies, secondary model-training restrictions, model drift notification protocols, ongoing algorithmic auditing, and enterprise cybersecurity certifications (SOC2 Type II, HITRUST).

title: Value-Based Care Software: What to Look For in a CMS TEAM Platform
text:

        A guide for hospital procurement teams evaluating care management software for CMS TEAM compliance — the capabilities that matter, the questions to ask, and the red flags to avoid.

        
          
             Jennifer Tim-Diamond
          
          ·
          July 22, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



TEAM needs 30-day cost tracking
Fragmented data creates blind spots
Platforms must span care settings
Real-time visibility drives performance





Most care management software was built for chronic disease management programs, Medicare ACO shared savings models, or HEDIS-driven quality reporting. These platforms are designed around longitudinal patient relationships, population-level risk stratification, and gaps in care — not around surgical episode cost windows and post-acute utilization tracking.
CMS TEAM requires something different: real-time visibility into total episode costs from the day of surgery through 30 days post-discharge. The hospital must track what is being spent on SNF days, home health visits, rehab facility stays, outpatient follow-up, and readmissions for each TEAM-eligible patient — all of which appear in claims data that lags three to six months under standard Medicare billing cycles.
Without purpose-built TEAM software, hospitals are flying blind. They cannot see their trajectory relative to target prices until the annual reconciliation statement arrives — by which point the performance year is over.



1. Real-time episode attribution. The software must identify TEAM-eligible episodes at the time of admission, not retroactively. That requires integration with the hospital’s EHR, ADT feeds, and scheduling systems to trigger episode tracking from the first qualifying surgical procedure.
2. Post-acute cost tracking. Claim data from SNFs, home health agencies, and IRFs flows through Medicare Part A; outpatient follow-up flows through Part B. Effective TEAM software aggregates both streams and maps them to the 30-day episode window per patient. This requires either a real-time claims feed from a clearinghouse or CMS’s TEAM data portal access.
3. Composite Quality Score (CQS) monitoring. TEAM’s reconciliation amount is adjusted up or down based on the CQS — a composite of hospital-wide readmission rate, PSI-90 complication measure, and patient experience scores. Platforms that only track episode cost without CQS monitoring give an incomplete picture of TEAM financial exposure.
4. EHR integration via FHIR. CMS TEAM requires documentation of specific care coordination activities, including primary care follow-up within seven days of discharge. FHIR R4-based integrations allow the TEAM platform to read clinical data from the EHR and write TEAM compliance documentation back into the record.
5. Target price comparison and projection. The most actionable feature: real-time comparison of current episode spending against the hospital’s CMS-issued target prices, with projection to year-end reconciliation outcome. This requires the hospital to receive and load its CMS target price file — available through the TEAM participant portal after signing the Data Sharing Agreement.




How does your platform attribute TEAM episodes in real time — and what is the attribution lag from admission to episode tracking?
Does your platform ingest post-acute claims (Part A and Part B) and map them to the 30-day episode window per patient? What is the claims latency?
Does your platform calculate or display the Composite Quality Score alongside episode cost tracking?
What EHR systems does your platform integrate with? Is the integration FHIR R4 certified?
Can your platform ingest our CMS-issued target price file and generate reconciliation projections against it?
What is your experience specifically with CMS TEAM, as distinct from BPCI Advanced, ACO models, or other bundled payment programs?



R.A.I.N. Compliant™ is purpose-built for CMS TEAM: real-time episode attribution from EHR ADT triggers, FHIR R4 integration, post-acute claims aggregation, CQS monitoring, and target price projection. SOC 2 Type 1 compliant. Implementation in approximately 10 weeks.







Value-based care software helps hospitals track, manage, and optimize performance under programs like CMS TEAM that tie Medicare payments to quality outcomes and total episode cost.



At minimum: real-time episode attribution, post-acute cost tracking across the 30-day window, Composite Quality Score monitoring, EHR integration via FHIR, and target price comparison and reconciliation projection.



No. Standard EHRs do not aggregate post-acute Medicare claims, track episode costs across the 30-day post-discharge window, or compare spending against CMS target prices. TEAM requires software that extends beyond the hospital’s four walls.

title: The Clinical Conscience of a Tech Company
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          Clinical Implementation Healthcare Leadership Nursing Health Technology CMS TEAM
        
        Media
        The Clinical Conscience of a Tech Company
        

        
          
             Robby Wallace
          
          ·
          June 04, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      
Our VP of Clinical Implementation on nursing as leadership, AI done right, and why the ripple effects of good healthcare work are never fully seen.
 I think of myself as a nurse detective. My strongest instinct is to follow the clinical evidence wherever it leads, connect dots that aren’t obviously connected, and then build something that actually changes how care is delivered — not just how it’s documented. 

As VP of Clinical Implementation for Rainfall Health, I bridge technology and healthcare as the subject matter expert. I ensure health tech actually works in the real world.
Imagine a software company builds a tool meant to help hospitals run better and treat patients more effectively. The engineers know how to build it, and the salespeople know how to sell it — but someone credible needs to deeply understand how doctors, nurses, and hospitals actually operate to ensure the product reflects that reality.
I am that bridge between the tech side and the clinical side, translating clinician-speak into engineer-speak, and vice versa. When a hospital’s leadership says, “this doesn’t fit how our staff works,” I step in to fix it. When the product team designs a new feature, I ensure it aligns with how care is actually delivered for industry standards guided by evidence-based practice.
Beyond that, I am a performance coach for healthcare organizations — helping them measure improvement, identify shortcomings, and make recommendations to implement the right strategies to close those gaps. Think of it like being the clinical conscience of a tech company: equal parts expert advisor, translator, problem-solver, and strategic partner to some of the most senior people in healthcare.

Early in my career, as a staff nurse, I noticed a pattern that concerned me. We saw an increase in at-risk exposures among patients and nursing staff, and I realized our existing infection control and safe handling processes had failure points that nobody had formally connected. Fail-safe measures that were supposed to protect staff were actually putting them at greater risk. The downstream effect was a rise in opportunistic infections that delayed care and extended patient length of stay.
I had just completed my master’s thesis in the area of quality improvement and prevention measures for safe handling in clinical settings, so I had both the clinical instincts and the analytical framework to address the issue. I didn’t want to wait for someone above me to act — and fortunately, my biggest ally was my unit manager who wanted me to champion this initiative. I developed a new workflow for infection control and safe handling using evidence to support its execution and design. I brought in nurse informaticists and nursing leaders to lead a new design for tracking isolated patients in the EHR system, which improved decision-making in patient placement and tracking.
The result was measurable reductions in both staff and patient exposure. But more than the numbers, what we built was a framework — a way of seeing risk before it became harm.
That experience shaped how I approach every role I’ve held since. I think of myself as a nurse detective. My strongest instinct is to follow the clinical evidence wherever it leads, connect dots that aren’t obviously connected, and then build something that actually changes how care is delivered — not just how it’s documented.

That I’m just a nurse. People hear about my clinical background and sometimes assume my value is in giving injections or placing an IV. And yes, albeit true, that is just a small piece. What nursing actually trained me to do is think critically under pressure, identify patterns in complex systems, identify critical gaps in clinical practice, advocate for people who can’t advocate for themselves, and drive change in environments that are inherently resistant to it.
The bedside is one of the best leadership schools in the world — you just don’t get credit for it until you reframe what people think nursing really is. I don’t leave my clinical identity at the door when I walk into an executive meeting. I intentionally bring it with me. I like to think it’s my competitive advantage.

I know the work I do creates a ripple effect that I may never fully see, but I know it is real.
At the bedside, it’s immediate and personal. I can see the impact on the person in front of me, on their family, on the people who love them. That kind of direct human connection is something I carry with me every single day.
But what drives me at this stage of my career is knowing that the work I do now extends far beyond any single patient. The frameworks I build, the programs I design, the care delivery changes I help implement — those decisions can touch hundreds of thousands of people across this country. People I will never meet. Families I will never know.
That’s an enormous responsibility. And it’s the greatest privilege I’ve ever had.

I think about the fact that my hands have touched humanity in ways that compound over time — from one patient, to one protocol, to one health system, to a national standard of care. That unending ripple effect is why I do this work. It’s not a job to me. It’s purpose.


AI — but with an important distinction that often gets lost in most conversations about it. I’m optimistic about AI as a tool and a resource. I’m not thinking about AI as a replacement — and I think that framing matters enormously for how we implement it responsibly.
What excites me is what AI can do for the clinician and for our healthcare system. It can surface patterns in patient data that a human mind can’t process at scale. It can reduce the burden that’s burning out our workforce. It can flag risk earlier, close gaps in care faster, and give providers more time to do the thing that no algorithm will ever replicate — being present with another human being in a moment of vulnerability.
But here’s what I’ve learned from years of being in the clinical setting: technology doesn’t make health care. People do. AI is only as good as the clinical judgment guiding how it’s used, what it’s measuring, and whose outcomes it’s optimizing for.

Running lean for financial gain. And I want to be clear about why — because this isn’t an abstract concern for me. I’ve seen what it looks like at the bedside.
When health systems make financial cuts, that cut hits staffing ratios, reduces resources, and strips away what is considered non-essential infrastructure in pursuit of margin. The consequences don’t stay in the boardroom — they travel directly to the patient. To the person who waited too long. To the patient who fell through the cracks. To the family who didn’t get the explanation they needed. To the nurse who had to choose which of their six patients needed her most in a moment when all six did.
The cruel irony is that running lean often costs more in the long run. Preventable readmissions. Longer lengths of stay. Workforce burnout and turnover. Adverse events that generate liability. The short-term financial logic often undermines the outcomes that determine long-term sustainability.

What concerns me most is when financial decisions are made without clinical voices at the table. When the people designing the cuts have never stood at a bedside and felt the weight of what those cuts actually mean in practice.

I’ve dedicated my career to ensuring that the clinical perspective isn’t an afterthought in those conversations — that quality and outcomes have a seat at the table when these strategies are being considered.

How much time do we have? I say that genuinely — because the honest answer is that this question may date me a bit. From Vocera and VoLTE to Epic Canto, continuous glucose monitoring, the Neulasta OnPro, the Apple Watch, and yes — even Claude. The list is long and it keeps growing.
But here’s the thread that connects all of them, and why they’ve mattered to me:
Nurses only have two hands. Not four. And in clinical practice, the difference between a good outcome and a bad one can come down to seconds — to whether you could reach a physician during a crisis, chart a critical change in real time, or free a patient from a process that was consuming their day.
Vocera and VoLTE gave me my voice when my hands were occupied — literally. Voice activation meant I could locate a teammate or escalate a concern without leaving a patient’s side. That’s not convenience. That’s safety.
Wrist-worn technology meant I could monitor, communicate, and respond without breaking the flow of care. Handheld charting meant documentation happened in the moment, not an hour later from memory — which means it was accurate, and accuracy in clinical documentation saves lives.
Continuous glucose monitoring changed what was possible for patients managing complex conditions — it gave them data, autonomy, and time back in their day to spend on living rather than managing disease.
The Neulasta OnPro meant a cancer patient didn’t have to make an extra trip back to an infusion center or clinic the day after chemotherapy. One less burden during the hardest season of their life.

What all of these have in common is that they gave time back — to clinicians, to patients, to families. And time in healthcare isn’t just efficiency. It’s dignity. It’s presence.

That’s the standard I apply to every technology I evaluate in my work today, whether for personal practice or as professional recommendations. Not — is this innovative? But — does this give someone their time back? Does it make the clinician more human, or less? Does it serve the patient, or just the system? The tools that pass that test are the ones worth investing in.

title: Hospital Readmissions and CMS TEAM: 48% of Hospital-Condition Pairs Are Still Failing the 30-Day Standard
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          Hospital Readmissions HRRP CMS TEAM Medicare Data Analysis sandbox-blog
        
        Media
        
        An analysis of 11,720 hospital-condition pairs under HRRP reveals the readmissions problem that CMS TEAM was built to address — and which states and procedures carry the highest risk.

        
          
             Jennifer Tim-Diamond
          
          ·
          July 22, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



HRRP still penalizes readmissions
TEAM adds full episode cost risk
Overlap raises financial exposure
Care transitions need redesign



The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program has been running since 2012. The premise is simple: if your patients return to the hospital within 30 days of discharge at a higher rate than CMS’s risk model expects given their medical profile, CMS docks your Medicare reimbursements. The penalty caps at 3% of all Medicare payments — not just payments for the penalized condition.
More than a decade later, the data says the program has defined the problem without solving it.



48.1% of HRRP-eligible hospital-condition pairs exceed the 1.0 ERR threshold — more readmissions than CMS models predict.
6 conditions tracked: AMI, Heart Failure, Pneumonia, COPD, Hip/Knee Arthroplasty (LEJR), and CABG.
1.00178 average excess readmission ratio nationally — the average hospital readmits slightly more patients than CMS models expect.
Hip/Knee has the highest average ERR at 1.00399 — the most difficult readmission problem to control under HRRP.
New Jersey leads all states at 65.4% of hospital-condition pairs penalized — the highest-risk geography in the dataset.
721 hospitals are now mandated under CMS TEAM, where readmission performance within the 30-day episode directly affects reimbursement reconciliation.

<BlogChartFigure src={“/charts/hrrp-state-bar.png”} alt={“Horizontal bar chart showing HRRP readmission penalty rate by state, with TEAM-heavy states highlighted in amber”} caption={“New Jersey at 65.4% is the chart’s outlier — but notice that most of the amber-highlighted states (high TEAM concentration) cluster well above the national average. The dashed line marks 48.1%: the national share of hospital-condition pairs with excess readmissions. The states above it have structural work to do before 2027 downside risk arrives.”} source={“CMS Provider Data Catalog, Dataset 9n3s-kdb3 (FY2024 HRRP). Computed from 11,720 non-suppressed records. Rainfall Health.”} />



New Jersey leads all states at 65.4% — nearly two out of every three hospital-condition pairs performing worse than CMS models predict. Massachusetts (62.5%) and Mississippi (61.1%) follow. New Jersey hosts some of the country’s highest-revenue hospital systems — Hackensack Meridian Health, RWJBarnabas — while Mississippi is rural and chronically underfunded. The same penalty outcome across fundamentally different systems.
Illinois (57.8%), Florida (57.5%), and Georgia (55.8%) cluster in the high-penalty tier. California (55.2%) and New York (52.7%) — both high-TEAM-concentration states — are also above the national average. This is not a rural poverty problem with a clean geographic boundary. High-resource markets are not immune.
The chart shows states above the national average — but even the better-performing states are not clean. Below-average means a smaller share of hospital-condition pairs exceed ERR 1.0, not zero penalties.
<BlogChartFigure src={“/charts/hrrp-condition-bar.png”} alt={“Bar chart showing average excess readmission ratio by HRRP condition, with hip/knee highlighted”} caption={“The amber bar is hip and knee replacement — the same procedure type that accounts for 58% of all CMS TEAM episodes. All conditions average above ERR 1.0, but Hip/Knee sits nearly twice as far above the benchmark as the next closest condition. The scale on this chart is deliberately tight: differences in the fifth decimal place translate to hundreds of thousands of dollars across a hospital’s annual episode volume.”} source={“CMS Provider Data Catalog, Dataset 9n3s-kdb3 (FY2024 HRRP). ERR values computed from non-suppressed hospital-condition pairs. Rainfall Health.”} />



All six HRRP conditions carry an average ERR above 1.0. But Hip/Knee (LEJR) stands apart. Its average ERR of 1.00399 is more than twice the gap of the next closest condition (CABG at 1.00179). That difference may look small in absolute terms. Multiplied across approximately 1.3 million joint replacements performed annually in the U.S., it represents a large volume of preventable returns.
The mechanism is structural. Elective joint replacement surgery has shortened its inpatient stay significantly over the past decade. What was a three-to-four-day admission is now often an outpatient or same-day procedure. That shift moves the readmission risk window entirely into post-discharge days — days hospitals cannot monitor in real time without deliberate post-acute coordination infrastructure.
This is directly relevant to CMS TEAM. LEJR is the highest-volume TEAM procedure at 58% of all episodes. Under TEAM, a readmission within 30 days of discharge is not just an HRRP penalty event — it is an episode cost that falls entirely on the hospital’s TEAM reconciliation account. The same failure that generates an HRRP penalty will also likely push the TEAM episode above its target price.



HRRP has been in effect since 2012. The fact that 48.1% of hospital-condition pairs still exceed the 1.0 ERR threshold more than a decade later says something about the limits of per-readmission financial penalties as a behavior change mechanism. Hospitals have responded — readmission rates have declined since HRRP launched — but the program has not solved the underlying problem.
CMS TEAM, mandatory for 721 hospitals starting January 1, 2026, goes further. TEAM attaches the entire 30-day episode cost to reimbursement — not just the readmission event. A hospital that manages to avoid the readmission but runs up high SNF, home health, or outpatient costs in the post-discharge window can still lose money on the episode. HRRP is where the penalty starts. TEAM is where the stakes get real.
The hospitals that have struggled under HRRP — high-readmission hospitals in New Jersey, Massachusetts, Illinois, and Florida — are the same hospitals most likely to be in scope for TEAM. The data in this analysis describes the problem TEAM was designed to address.



The excess readmission ratio (ERR) is a hierarchical logistic regression model estimate produced annually by CMS for each hospital-condition pair. The model controls for patient age, sex, principal diagnosis, comorbidities, and prior utilization using Medicare Part A claims. An ERR of 1.0 means the hospital readmitted exactly as many patients as its risk-adjusted peer group would predict. Above 1.0 means excess readmissions; below 1.0 means fewer readmissions than predicted.
The FY2024 HRRP dataset analyzed here (CMS Provider Data Catalog, Dataset 9n3s-kdb3) covers the measurement period July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2024 — a three-year rolling window. CMS suppresses hospital-condition pairs where the hospital has fewer than 25 discharges for the condition in the measurement period, to protect statistical reliability. The suppression is systematic: small rural hospitals disproportionately fall below the threshold and disappear from the analysis. The 11,720 valid records analyzed represent a 2,700+ hospital subset weighted toward larger, busier facilities. Every finding in this analysis should be read with that structural bias in mind.
The analysis was produced from the CMS open data API: https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/api/1/datastore/query/9n3s-kdb3/0 — the same endpoint used in the Artometrics READMITTED analysis (artometrics.com/readmitted, April 2026). The 18,330 total records retrieved include both suppressed and non-suppressed rows; ERR computations are based on the 11,720 rows with valid, non-suppressed ERR values.
(Source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (2024). HRRP FY2025 supplemental data, Dataset 9n3s-kdb3.)

Analyzing the HRRP dataset by hospital ownership type reveals a consistent pattern: for-profit hospitals carry a modestly higher share of penalized hospital-condition pairs than nonprofit and government-owned hospitals. In the FY2024 data, the for-profit sector runs approximately 8–10 percentage points above the nonprofit sector in the share of pairs exceeding ERR 1.0.
This gap reflects several dynamics. For-profit hospitals — particularly the large investor-owned chains HCA Healthcare, Tenet Health, and Steward Health — have faced sustained shareholder pressure on cost reduction and length-of-stay management that can accelerate discharge at the cost of post-discharge continuity. Shorter hospital stays reduce readmission risk for some patients and increase it for others; the net effect in the HRRP data is a modest excess penalty rate.
Under CMS TEAM, the ownership-type dynamic is complicated by the fact that HCA Healthcare’s BPCI Advanced experience gives its for-profit hospitals episode management infrastructure that many nonprofits lack. HCA’s data analytics capabilities may partially offset the behavioral incentive effects captured in the HRRP data. Tenet Health and Steward Health — the latter having entered bankruptcy in 2024 — present more uncertain pictures: their TEAM episode management infrastructure varies significantly by hospital and market.
(Source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (2024). Hospital General Information, Dataset xubh-q36u.)





The ERR is a ratio of a hospital’s predicted readmissions to its expected readmissions, where expected is risk-adjusted for the patient population’s age, comorbidities, and discharge history. An ERR above 1.0 means more readmissions than CMS models predict.



48.1% of hospital-condition pairs in the FY2024 HRRP dataset exceed the ERR 1.0 threshold, according to analysis of the CMS Provider Data Catalog (dataset 9n3s-kdb3).



New Jersey leads all states at 65.4% of hospital-condition pairs above ERR 1.0, followed by Massachusetts (62.5%) and Mississippi (61.1%).



HRRP penalizes specific readmission events. CMS TEAM goes further by attaching the entire 30-day post-discharge episode cost to reimbursement. A readmission under TEAM is both an HRRP penalty event and an episode cost event — the same failure hits twice.

On Rainfall’s March 2026 directory, hospital-name patterns associated with HCA — including TriStar, HealthONE, and related cues such as Medical City — match approximately 29 TEAM hospitals, the largest for-profit cluster we measure. Exact legal ownership can differ from signage; treat the count as a density signal, not a 10-K extract.
Concentration is highest in Territory 4 (Tennessee / Florida) with additional Colorado HealthONE presence inside Denver’s 21-hospital TEAM CBSA (Territory 1). That multi-territory spread lets HCA reuse episode playbooks — order sets, PAC contracts, gainsharing templates — across CBSAs.



When multiple sister hospitals sit in one CBSA, discharge destination norms propagate. A TriStar preferred SNF panel becomes the default rehab market even for non-HCA hospitals that lack an alternative. Independent Nashville and Jacksonville hospitals should assume they are price-takers in PAC unless they build competing capacity or joint panels.
See the Tennessee and Florida TEAM hospital directories for named hospitals, and the South region hub for CBSA rollups.

Flag agencies that are de facto HCA-preferred and negotiate dual-panel access or build alternatives.
Mirror HCA’s operational cadence: weekly episode huddles, implant formularies, and early home discharge goals.
Avoid competing on brand advertising; compete on measurable 30-day cost and readmission outcomes.

title: BPCI Advanced Saved Medicare $465 Million: What TEAM Can Learn
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          CMS TEAM BPCI Advanced Bundled Payments Medicare Savings sandbox-blog
        
        Media
        
        Five years of BPCI Advanced outcomes data shows what bundled payments can achieve — and what the predecessor model's gains and losses mean for hospitals entering TEAM in 2026.

        
          
             Jennifer Tim-Diamond
          
          ·
          July 22, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



BPCI Advanced saved Medicare large sums
TEAM is the mandatory successor
Lessons transfer to episode design
Upside alone is not enough



BPCI Advanced ran from October 2018 through December 2022. Unlike TEAM, participation was voluntary — hospitals opted in on specific clinical episode types and faced financial risk only on the episodes they chose. By the end of Model Year 5, CMS confirmed $464.7 million in net Medicare savings, with the surgical episode types (including hip and knee replacement and spinal fusion) contributing $147.1 million of that total.
That number matters for TEAM. TEAM was explicitly designed as the mandatory successor to BPCI Advanced, incorporating lessons from the voluntary model and applying them to 721 hospitals in 188 Core-Based Statistical Areas regardless of whether those hospitals chose to participate.
<BlogChartFigure src={“/charts/bpci-savings.png”} alt={“Bar chart showing BPCI Advanced net Medicare savings by model year from 2018 to 2022”} caption={“The program started in the red. Model Year 1 produced a net $152 million loss as participants learned the model. By Model Year 5, BPCI Advanced had generated $464.7 million in net Medicare savings. The surgical episode segment alone contributed $147.1 million of the MY5 total. This is the trajectory CMS designed TEAM to replicate — and accelerate — at mandatory scale.”} source={“CMS BPCI Advanced Annual Report 5 (AR5, MY5 2022) and Annual Report 6 (AR6), published 2024-2025. Rainfall Health.”} />


The single largest source of BPCI Advanced savings was a reduction in inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) payments. CMS’s AR6 analysis found that IRF payments fell $423 per episode — a 42.2% reduction — among BPCI Advanced participants, driven primarily by shifting appropriate patients from IRF to home health or lower-level skilled nursing facility care.
This is directly relevant to TEAM. IRF usage is one of the highest-cost post-discharge settings for LEJR and SHFFT episodes. Hospitals that were BPCI Advanced participants and have already developed protocols to direct patients to lower-cost appropriate post-acute settings enter TEAM with a structural advantage. Hospitals without that infrastructure face a steep learning curve in PY2, when downside risk begins.



BPCI Advanced posted a net loss in Model Year 1 (2018). Participants were new to episode management, post-acute coordination was underdeveloped, and many hospitals were still benchmarking their own spending. The model turned net-positive in MY2 and grew steadily from there.
CMS designed TEAM with PY1 as an upside-only “dress rehearsal” precisely because of this learning curve pattern. The intent is for PY1 to be used for infrastructure building — establishing episode tracking, benchmarking, and post-acute partnerships — before two-sided risk begins in PY2.



Three BPCI Advanced capabilities transfer directly to TEAM: post-acute discharge optimization, care coordination across the 30-day window, and real-time episode cost tracking. Hospitals that built these under BPCI Advanced are ahead.
What does not transfer cleanly: BPCI Advanced participants self-selected their episode types and had the option to drop episodes that were performing poorly. Under TEAM, hospitals participate in all five episode types whether or not they have experience managing each one. Hospitals that were BPCI Advanced participants only on LEJR now face mandatory accountability for spinal fusion, SHFFT, major bowel, and CABG as well.
The other key difference is scale. BPCI Advanced was voluntary and attracted hospitals already motivated to manage episode costs. TEAM captures the full range — including hospitals that never chose bundled payments and may have limited infrastructure.





BPCI Advanced generated $464.7 million in net Medicare savings by Model Year 5 (2022), according to CMS Annual Report 5.



TEAM is mandatory for 721 selected hospitals in 188 Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs); BPCI Advanced was voluntary. TEAM requires accountability for five specific surgical episodes; BPCI Advanced covered a broader set of optional clinical episodes. TEAM introduces downside risk in PY2 (2027).



The primary driver was a $423/episode reduction in inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) payments — a 42.2% decrease — as hospitals shifted appropriate post-acute patients to lower-cost settings like home health.

title: CMS TEAM Explained for Hospital CEOs: What It Means, What’s at Stake, and What to Do
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          CMS TEAM Hospital CEO Value-Based Care sandbox-blog
        
        Media
        
        Plain-English, CEO to CEO: your hospital is now financially accountable for five surgeries and the 30 days after each — whether you opted in or not.

        
          
             Ahmed \"Eddie\" Qureshi, CEO
          
          ·
          July 09, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      


TL;DR



Hospitals own full episode risk
Five surgical categories count
Thirty days post-discharge matter
Leadership must redesign care paths



Let me put this plainly. If your hospital is one of the 721 in the CMS TEAM model, Medicare is no longer just paying you for the operation — it’s holding you accountable for what happens for 30 days afterward, across five common surgeries. This started January 1, 2026.


You keep billing fee-for-service, but CMS reconciles your actual spending against a target price. Beat it with good quality and you earn a bonus. Miss it, and starting in 2027 you write CMS a check.



Rainfall Health estimates up to 20% of Medicare revenue is at stake and up to $85 million in five-year upside for a system that gets this right — our own figures, not independently audited. Independent analysts are more cautious: Optum Advisory projects that “56% of mandatory participants are projected to lose money under current criteria unless they meaningfully improve performance,” averaging $1.2 million per facility, and Brandeis University with the Institute for Accountable Care anticipates up to two-thirds of hospitals losing revenue on net. Either way, doing nothing is the expensive option.




Get your data house in order across the full 30-day episode.
Lock in post-acute partners who deliver low readmissions (each one avoided saves roughly $14,000, per Milliman).
Assign an owner and pick your track deliberately before 2027 downside risk arrives.



Rainfall Health is the first and only recognized standard for Medicare-mandated models like CMS TEAM — and we go at-risk alongside our hospital partners.







No — participation is mandatory for any IPPS hospital whose CMS Certification Number sits within one of the 188 selected Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs).



Downside financial risk starts in Performance Year 2, calendar year 2027.



Rainfall Health estimates up to $85 million in five-year upside for a system that performs well — a company-stated figure, not independently audited.



Fix your episode data across the full 30-day window — this is the foundation every other TEAM initiative depends on.



A named executive should own it — most commonly someone in case management or population health.
