title: Rainfall Health Submits Comments on CMS Proposed Rules for CJR-X and TEAM, Applauding the Continued Move to Value-Based Payment
text:
Back to Blogs & Media
      

      
        
          CMS TEAM CJR-X value-based care Medicare episode payment
        
        Media
        
        

        
          
             Christina Keny
          
          ·
          June 17, 2026

          
            
              
            
            
              
            
            
          
        
      

      

      
On June 8, 2026, Rainfall Health submitted formal comment letters to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) on two proposed rules that together represent the next chapter of Medicare’s transition from fee-for-service to episode value-based accountability: the proposed CJR-X Model and the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS Proposed Rule (CMS-1849-P), which includes proposed changes to the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) Composite Quality Score (CQS) methodology and a Request for Information on extending TEAM to ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs).


TL;DR



Rainfall supports mandatory CJR-X and TEAM accountability
Comments urge stronger risk adjustment and PRO-PM weighting
TEAM CQS should reward timely improvement, not lag alone
ASC expansion needs clear attribution before PY3
Full PDF letters are linked at the end of this article



We applaud CMS’s continued leadership in advancing value-based payment. Both rules reflect a federal commitment to rewarding healthcare systems that deliver coordinated, patient-centered surgical care across the full perioperative episode, and both create a meaningful opportunity to improve outcomes for Medicare beneficiaries, particularly those served by safety-net, rural, Medicare-Dependent, and Sole Community Hospitals.


The stakes of getting these models right have never been higher. The Medicare population is aging rapidly, and with that demographic shift comes a proportional rise in surgical volume among older adults. Older adults face an elevated risk of mortality and morbidity following surgery owing to comorbidities and age-related physiological changes. These are not the lower-acuity surgical patients of a decade ago — they are patients whose recovery trajectory is determined as much by what happens in the 30 to 90 days after surgical discharge, at the SNF, at home, in the primary care follow-up, as by what happens in the operating room. They require specialized perioperative pathways, structured care coordination across multiple settings, and reliable information transfer between every clinician who touches the episode of care. Fee-for-service reimbursement was never designed to pay for that work. Mandatory, episode-based, value-based payment models are.
That is why the mandatory nature of CJR-X and TEAM matters. Voluntary models will not propel the changes needed to support all patients — particularly those with the greatest medical and social complexity. Mandatory, nationwide participation closes that gap. It ensures that the safety-net, rural, Medicare-Dependent, and Sole Community Hospitals serving the most complex Medicare beneficiaries are brought into the same accountability of quality care framework.
Equally important, both CJR-X and TEAM reflect a deliberate elevation of patient-reported outcomes alongside traditional surgical quality metrics. Through the THA/TKA PRO-PM, the Information Transfer PRO-PM, and the broader emphasis on functional recovery, CMS is signaling that surgical success is no longer measured solely by 30-day readmissions or mortality. It is measured by whether the patient can climb their stairs, manage their medications, and live independently in the weeks and months after surgery. That is the right standard for an aging population, and it is the standard Rainfall Health is built to help healthcare systems meet through their AI platform.



Rainfall Health supports the proposed nationwide, mandatory expansion of CJR-X, including the preservation of the 90-day episode window, the differentiated stop-loss/stop-gain limits (5% for safety-net, rural, Medicare-Dependent, and Sole Community Hospitals; 20% for all others), and the inclusion of outpatient lower-extremity joint replacement procedures. An independent CJR evaluation found that participating hospitals reduced average episode payments by approximately $1,000 per episode, driven primarily by more appropriate post-acute utilization rather than reductions in clinical quality, and the 90-day window is the structural feature most responsible for that measured behavior change. Shortening it would create incentives for premature discharge and truncate accountability before most complications surface.
To strengthen the model further, Rainfall Health recommended that CMS:

Strengthen risk adjustment for medically and socially complex beneficiaries by adopting peer-group benchmarking based on dual-eligible share and incorporating frailty indicators.
Protect first-time mandatory participants through a downside-risk glide path and targeted technical assistance for safety-net and rural hospitals.
Heavily weight the THA/TKA PRO-PM in the Composite Quality Score and standardize PROM instruments and EHR-extractable specifications.
Improve data timeliness and target-price transparency, including monthly claims feedback with ≤60-day lag and prospective target prices published before each performance year.
Align CJR-X with age-friendly and geriatric surgery priorities by extending the proposed in-home telehealth G-codes to 4Ms-aligned services (Mentation, Mobility, Medications, What Matters).




On TEAM, Rainfall Health strongly supports CMS’s proposed shift from a fixed historical baseline to a rolling baseline CQS methodology and the decision to build the CQS from data hospitals already submit under the IQR, OQR, and HAC Reduction programs. Surgical quality improves continuously, not in five-year intervals, and aligning the measurement framework with how clinical improvement actually occurs at the bedside is the right answer for Medicare beneficiaries. Reusing existing reporting infrastructure also preserves TEAM’s promise of reducing administrative burden, where every hour clinical staff spend on duplicative reporting is an hour not spent on the bedside coordination that drives 30-day outcomes.
We recommended three amendments to strengthen the patient-care impact of the CQS:

Shorten the lag between performance and CQS updates so that within-year improvements in readmissions, safety events, and care transitions are captured through hybrid claims plus eCQM data already submitted under IQR, and are reflected in the same Performance Year’s reconciliation.
Preserve both achievement and improvement scoring for at least Performance Years 1–3, with a minimum CQS floor for hospitals demonstrating defined year-over-year improvement, so that safety-net and high-acuity hospitals are not penalized for starting further behind.
Incorporate at least one cross-setting care coordination measure, such as documented 30-day home-time outcome, given that approximately 34% of total inpatient TEAM episode costs are incurred after discharge.

On the Request for Information regarding ASC inclusion, we support extending TEAM to ASCs beginning no earlier than PY3 (CY 2028), but only after CMS resolves four structural issues: adverse selection driven by site-of-care migration, ASC-specific risk-adjusted episode benchmarks, ASC-adapted quality measure development, and clear prospective episode attribution rules. We also urged CMS to publish a comprehensive TEAM Year 1 analysis before finalizing ASC expansion.



The shift to episode-based payment models like TEAM is exposing a fundamental gap in how healthcare systems collect quality and care coordination data as well as how they manage performance. Traditional manual data collection and retrospective reporting built on delayed claims and fragmented data cannot support real time clinical and operational decision making. By the time performance gaps are identified, the opportunity to impact outcomes and costs has already passed.
Rainfall Health closes this gap with an AI native platform designed for real time episode management. By continuously integrating clinical and operational data, Rainfall delivers live visibility into patient trajectories, projected episode costs, and quality performance, enabling care teams to take action when it matters most during the episode itself.
At the core of the platform is a unified approach to clinical operations and value-based performance. Rainfall combines episode cost analytics, quality measure monitoring, post-acute network optimization, and seamless care coordination across hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, home health, and primary care. This transforms the 30- and 90-day surgical episode from a disconnected series of retroactive encounters into a continuously managed, real-time data driven care journey.
The platform identifies the within episode drivers of performance such as readmission risk, post-acute placement decisions, care transition gaps, and PROM completion, and translates them into point of care guidance for clinicians and operational teams. Rainfall Health partners with hospitals across all five TEAM procedures and a diverse range of care environments, from large health systems to safety net, rural, Medicare Dependent, and Sole Community Hospitals. The AI platform is built to align with real world workflows, enabling organizations to operationalize value-based care and not just report on it.
As CMS accelerates the move toward episode-based accountability, success will depend on the ability to manage risk in real time, coordinate care across settings, and act on insights at the point of care. Rainfall Health is purpose built to help hospitals do exactly that, turning value-based care from a reporting exercise into a core operational capability.

title: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.
text:
Newsletter




Los Angeles stayed a mandatory market under an older Medicare bundled-payment program for nine straight years, specifically because it was expensive. San Francisco got downgraded to voluntary in 2018. Under TEAM’s own, separate lottery, LA drew exactly one hospital — voluntarily. San Francisco drew 37 — mandatorily, the most of any market in California.


Rainfall Health · September 2026

title: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.
section: The three California markets, before and after
text:
The three California markets, before and after
California had three markets in CJR’s original 67-MSA lottery: Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward (renamed San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont under the 2023 OMB delineation), and Modesto. All three were mandatory when CJR launched in 2016. In 2018, CMS cut mandatory participation to the 34 MSAs with the highest historical episode spending — a cost-based cut, not a second lottery. LA’s spending was high enough to stay in. San Francisco’s and Modesto’s weren’t; both dropped to voluntary.
Six years later, TEAM ran its own, unrelated stratified draw across the whole country. The outcome for these same three markets:









Market
CJR status (2018+)
TEAM hospitals
TEAM participation




Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim
Mandatory
1 (Cedars-Sinai)

LA is the market this newsletter has already covered in depth: the country’s largest Medicare market, drawn out of TEAM’s mandatory lottery, with its one hospital — Cedars-Sinai — there entirely by its own election. What hadn’t been checked until now is what happened to the other two California markets that went through the same CJR history. The answer isn’t “the same bad luck twice.” San Francisco has more TEAM hospitals than any other market in California, mandatorily, and Modesto simply isn’t on the list.

title: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.
section: Zooming out from three markets to sixty-seven
text:
Zooming out from three markets to sixty-seven
Three markets is an anecdote. The full CJR roster — all 67 MSAs from the original 2016 lottery — is a real sample. CMS no longer publishes the 2018 list of 34 mandatory MSAs as a single named table (its current CJR hospital list mixes mandatory and voluntary-continuing hospitals with no status column), so this analysis reconstructs it: re-applying CMS’s own stated 2018 criterion — highest average wage-adjusted historical episode payment — to the original 67-MSA roster, using CMS’s own 2015-rule payment data. The reconstruction reproduces all three known outcomes above as a check on itself before being used for anything else.
Against TEAM’s 188 selected CBSAs nationally (out of 803 total eligible CBSAs, metropolitan and micropolitan combined, under the current OMB delineation — a 23.4% baseline rate if the draw were blind to CJR history):



Group
Selected into TEAM
Rate




All 67 original CJR markets
19 of 67
28.4%


34 former-mandatory CJR markets
12 of 34
35.3%


33 former-voluntary-tier CJR markets
7 of 33
21.2%


National baseline (all eligible CBSAs)
188 of 803
23.4%



The corrected baseline changes the shape of the finding. Markets that went through CJR at all didn’t get a discount on TEAM’s lottery — if anything, they did slightly better than the national rate, 28.4% against a 23.4% baseline. And the split inside that group runs in one direction: the 34 markets CMS once forced into mandatory participation were selected at 35.3%, well above the national rate, while the 33 it let go voluntary landed close to it, at 21.2%. San Francisco isn’t an outlier inside this data — it’s sitting in the voluntary-tier group, which performed closest to what a blind national draw would predict. Los Angeles, in the higher-exposure mandatory tier, is the one whose individual outcome ran against its own group’s trend: that tier did better than average overall, and Los Angeles was still in the majority of it that didn’t land on TEAM’s roster.

title: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.
section: What this doesn’t establish
text:
What this doesn’t establish
TEAM’s selection, like CJR’s original lottery, is a stratified random draw — a result like this could reflect a real relationship between market characteristics and TEAM’s stratification variables (population, historical spending, something correlated with having been a large CJR market in the first place), or it could be within the ordinary noise of a draw this size. No significance test has been run on this, and none is claimed here. What can be said cleanly: in this one draw, the historical direction of “was CMS willing to force this market to participate before” ran toward more TEAM exposure, not less — the opposite of what a simple “same unlucky markets” story would predict, and the exact opposite of what happened to LA specifically inside its own market’s hospital count.
The 34-mandatory-MSA list itself is a reconstruction, not a CMS-published table copied verbatim — see “About the data” below before treating any single MSA’s status as certain.

title: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.
section: What’s still unverified
text:
What’s still unverified
Whether TEAM’s own stratification variables (the ones CMS used to draw its selected CBSAs) include anything that correlates mechanically with CJR history — population size and historical joint-replacement spending are plausible candidates, since both featured in CJR’s own stratification — hasn’t been checked. If TEAM’s strata happen to overlap with CJR’s, the pattern here could be a byproduct of both models drawing on similar underlying market characteristics rather than any information flow between the two programs. This would need TEAM’s own published stratification methodology cross-referenced against CJR’s, which hasn’t been done here.


About the data. TEAM hospital counts are computed at render time from the TEAM Participant List - 2026Q2 (as of April 15, 2026), the same file Medicare publishes as the official participant roster. The 34-mandatory-MSA list is a reconstruction built by applying CMS’s own stated 2018 selection criterion (highest wage-adjusted historical episode payment) to the original 67-MSA CJR roster, using CMS’s own 2015-rule payment data — CMS no longer publishes the 2018 list as a single named table. The reconstruction independently reproduces the three publicly documented outcomes for Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Modesto as a validity check. Full underlying data and methodology: essays/rainfall-team-cjrx-research/data/national-roster-findings.md in the working repository (supporting research material, not a published page). title: Two California Markets Have Exactly One TEAM Hospital Each — Because That’s All There Is
text:
Newsletter




Los Angeles has one hospital in Medicare’s TEAM model because a huge metro got skipped by the lottery and one CJR veteran volunteered in. Crescent City and Hanford-Corcoran have one hospital each too — for the opposite reason: there’s only one hospital in either market, and this time the lottery actually caught them.


Rainfall Health · September 2026
Los Angeles has exactly one hospital in Medicare’s newest mandatory payment program, and so do Miami and Tampa. In all three cases, the explanation is the same: CMS’s lottery skipped the metro area entirely, and one hospital with nine years of history in a prior mandatory bundle used a narrow rule to volunteer in anyway, while every other hospital in a market of millions sat out.
Two more California markets show the identical outcome — one hospital, the entire TEAM footprint for that metro — and it is tempting to assume the same mechanism is at work. It isn’t. Sutter Coast Hospital, in Crescent City, and Adventist Health Hanford, in Hanford-Corcoran, are mandatory TEAM participants because CMS’s lottery landed directly on their metro areas, not because it missed them. And each is the only hospital on the roster there for the plainest possible reason: each is the only acute-care hospital in the market, period.

title: Two California Markets Have Exactly One TEAM Hospital Each — Because That’s All There Is
section: What TEAM asks of a hospital
text:
What TEAM asks of a hospital
The Transforming Episode Accountability Model is a five-year Medicare program that makes a hospital financially responsible for the cost and outcomes of a patient’s care for 30 days after five kinds of surgery: hip and knee replacement, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass grafting, hip fracture repair, and major bowel surgery. 720 hospitals are on the roster. Selection isn’t by application — CMS divided the country into metropolitan and micropolitan areas, drew 188 of them by stratified random sample, and made every IPPS-paid acute-care hospital sitting inside a drawn area mandatory. A small number of hospitals outside the drawn areas can also join voluntarily, but only if they ran a mandatory CJR or BPCI Advanced bundle through its final months. That voluntary pathway is how Los Angeles, Miami, and Tampa each ended up with their one hospital.

title: Two California Markets Have Exactly One TEAM Hospital Each — Because That’s All There Is
section: Two markets, one hospital, same shape as LA — different cause
text:
Two markets, one hospital, same shape as LA — different cause
Sutter Coast Hospital (CCN 050417) sits in the Crescent City CBSA, CMS code 18860, one of the drawn areas. Adventist Health Hanford (CCN 050121) sits in the Hanford–Corcoran CBSA, CMS code 25260, also drawn. Sutter Coast Hospital is listed as a mandatory participant and Adventist Health Hanford as a mandatory participant — neither is a voluntary joiner, and neither is a late addition. CMS’s TEAM participant list marks both “N” for newly identified relative to the prior list, meaning neither is a recent addition; both have been on the roster since the program’s first performance year began January 1, 2026.
Each CBSA has exactly one hospital on the TEAM roster: 1 in Crescent City, 1 in Hanford–Corcoran. That much matches the shape of the LA/Miami/Tampa pattern. What doesn’t match is the reason. CMS’s Hospital General Information dataset — the same public registry that lists every Medicare-enrolled hospital in the country, filtered here to Del Norte County (where Crescent City sits) and Kings County (where Hanford, and its CBSA-mate Corcoran, sit) — shows exactly one acute-care hospital in each county, and it’s the same hospital in each case that’s already on the TEAM roster. Sutter Coast Hospital is the only Medicare-enrolled acute-care hospital anywhere in Del Norte County. Adventist Health Hanford is the only one in Kings County. Neither market has a second hospital that TEAM’s rule happened to catch or miss — there was never a second hospital to catch.
That also rules out the explanation this project flagged as worth checking first: a Critical Access Hospital quietly excluded from IPPS-based eligibility, leaving only one of several local hospitals mandatory by default. CMS’s own data classifies both Sutter Coast Hospital and Adventist Health Hanford as “Acute Care Hospitals,” not Critical Access Hospitals, and their CCNs (050417 and 050121) fall inside the 0001-0879 numbering block CMS reserves for short-term general and specialty hospitals — the same block as any other acute surgical hospital in the country, not the CAH-specific range. There is no excluded second hospital in either county to explain away. The one-hospital outcome here needs no exclusion mechanism at all; it’s just what the market looks like.
Neither hospital carries the CJR history that put Cedars-Sinai, Morton Plant, and the former Westchester General on the TEAM roster voluntarily. Checked directly against CMS’s own CJR hospital-list spreadsheets — the pre-February 2018 list and the July 2024 list, the model’s first and near-final rosters — neither CCN 050417 nor CCN 050121 appears on either one. Sutter Coast Hospital and Adventist Health Hanford are on TEAM because their metro areas were drawn, not because either was previously part of a mandatory bundle and chose to keep going.

title: Two California Markets Have Exactly One TEAM Hospital Each — Because That’s All There Is
section: The scale contrast is the opposite of LA’s
text:
The scale contrast is the opposite of LA’s
Los Angeles is the second-largest metro area in the country, with a Census-estimated population of roughly 12.9 million people; TEAM’s entire footprint there is one hospital that didn’t have to be there. Crescent City and Hanford-Corcoran run the comparison the other way. Del Norte County — the entirety of the Crescent City micropolitan area — had an estimated population of 27,009 as of July 1, 2024, according to the Census Bureau’s Vintage 2024 population estimates. Kings County, which is the entirety of the Hanford-Corcoran metropolitan area (Census classifies it as a full Metropolitan Statistical Area, not a micropolitan one, since its population clears the 50,000 threshold), had an estimated population of 154,913 the same year. Both are more than 80 times smaller than Los Angeles County’s metro population, and Crescent City’s is smaller than a single large hospital’s typical annual patient volume in a major city. TEAM’s rule doesn’t scale mandatory participation to market size — a hospital in a county of 27,000 people carries exactly the same one-hospital designation as a lottery-skipped hospital standing in for 12.9 million.

title: Two California Markets Have Exactly One TEAM Hospital Each — Because That’s All There Is
section: What isn’t established here
text:
What isn’t established here
This piece checked CJR history for both hospitals against CMS’s pre-2018 and July 2024 hospital-list spreadsheets; it did not run an equivalent check against BPCI Advanced’s participant rosters, which CMS does not publish in the same consolidated spreadsheet format. Given that both hospitals are listed as Mandatory rather than Voluntary participants, a BPCI Advanced history would not change how either landed on the roster — but it’s worth flagging as unverified rather than assumed. Separately, this piece did not attempt to determine why CMS’s stratified sampling weights happened to draw these two specific small markets rather than other similarly sized ones; that would require the underlying sampling-weight methodology CMS has not published market-by-market. And the fresh CMS participant-list pull used to verify hospital-level detail here (dated August 18, 2026, 722 hospitals) carries two more hospitals nationally than the vendored copy this article’s 720 figure is computed from (dated April 15, 2026, 720 hospitals) — both list Crescent City and Hanford-Corcoran identically, but the discrepancy is noted rather than reconciled.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
text:
Newsletter




Laguna Honda Hospital has no emergency room and, by CMS’s own quality data, performs none of the five surgeries Medicare’s TEAM model is built around. It’s on the mandatory roster anyway, for a reason that has nothing to do with what the hospital does.


Rainfall Health · September 2026
Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center is California’s largest public nursing home. It has no emergency department. It does not perform hip replacements, knee replacements, spinal fusions, heart bypass surgery, or major bowel surgery — the five procedures that CMS’s newest mandatory payment program, the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), exists to manage. It spent more than two years with no Medicare or Medicaid certification at all, after federal regulators shut off its funding in 2022 over safety violations.
It is also, as of January 1, 2026, a mandatory TEAM participant, on the hook for the cost and quality of surgeries it does not do.
That isn’t a data error on anyone’s part. It’s what happens when a fifty-year-old hospital license and a geography-based selection rule interact without anyone checking what the hospital behind the license actually does.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: What TEAM asks of a hospital
text:
What TEAM asks of a hospital
TEAM is a five-year Medicare program that makes a hospital financially responsible for the cost and outcomes of a patient’s care for 30 days after five kinds of surgery: lower-extremity joint replacement, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass grafting, surgical hip and femur fracture treatment, and major bowel procedures. 720 hospitals are on the roster, selected not by application but by CMS’s own rule: any hospital paid under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS), with a CMS Certification Number (CCN) address inside one of 188 metropolitan or micropolitan areas CMS drew by stratified random sample, is mandatory. There is no volume screen in that rule and no review of what a given hospital actually treats. If the hospital’s CCN sits in the right geography and the right regulatory category, it’s in.
Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center (CCN 050668) sits inside the San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont CBSA, one of the mandatory areas, alongside 36 other hospitals. That’s the entire mechanism. Nothing about its patient population or its surgical volume enters into it.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: A hospital that does almost none of what the model assumes
text:
A hospital that does almost none of what the model assumes
CMS’s own public data shows why that matters here specifically. In the Hospital General Information file CMS publishes for Care Compare, Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center is classified as an “Acute Care Hospital” and separately marked as offering no emergency services. In CMS’s Complications and Deaths dataset, eight distinct postoperative-complication measures tied to surgical inpatients — including postoperative hemorrhage, postoperative sepsis, postoperative respiratory failure, and wound dehiscence — are reported for Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center with the footnote “no cases met the criteria for this measure.” Its hip/knee replacement complication rate, and its 30-day mortality rates for CABG, heart attack, and stroke, carry no published rate at all. Its emergency-department volume measure is unreported for the same underlying reason: there isn’t an emergency department generating one.
UCSF’s Orthopaedic Surgery department, which staffs Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center, lists exactly three specialties there: physical medicine and rehabilitation, podiatry, and orthotics and prosthetics. No orthopedic surgeons. The hospital does still admit real, medically complex patients — CMS’s hybrid mortality measure shows 28 qualifying stays in its most recent period, and it reports real caseloads for sepsis-care and pneumonia measures — so this isn’t a hospital with no patients. It’s a hospital whose patients are not having the kind of surgery TEAM was built to track.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: Why a nursing-home-style hospital carries a surgical-hospital’s CCN
text:
Why a nursing-home-style hospital carries a surgical-hospital’s CCN
The explanation is bureaucratic, not clinical. CMS assigns CCNs by facility type in fixed numeric blocks, published in its own cost-report documentation: 0001-0879 for short-term general and specialty hospitals, 2000-2299 for long-term care hospitals (excluded from IPPS), 3025-3099 for rehabilitation hospitals (also excluded from IPPS). Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center’s CCN, 050668, falls inside the short-term general hospital block — the same block as every acute surgical hospital in the country — rather than in either of the two blocks reserved for facilities that function the way it actually does today.
That placement isn’t a clerical mistake CMS is unaware of; it’s the hospital’s actual, current Medicare enrollment category, and TEAM’s eligibility rule reads that category literally. A hospital paid under IPPS in a mandatory CBSA is in, full stop. Nothing in the rule asks whether a hospital with that license is still using it for surgery.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: A hospital that had no certification at all for two years
text:
A hospital that had no certification at all for two years
The mismatch is sharper because of what happened in between. In April 2022, CMS terminated Laguna Honda’s Medicare and Medicaid participation entirely, after inspections triggered by two self-reported, non-fatal overdoses on-site turned up broader safety violations — problems with medication handling, infection control, and site security. Federal officials gave the hospital months to close and transfer out its residents. The transfers themselves became controversial: the San Francisco Chronicle reported at least four resident deaths within days to weeks of transfer in mid-2022, and the California Department of Public Health issued a round of citations in December 2022 tied to a larger set of resident relocations, some of which it found were followed by death. Laguna Honda regained Medicaid certification in August 2023 and full Medicare certification in June 2024 — a gap of just over two years with no federal certification of any kind.
None of that history bears on surgical volume. It’s cited here because it underscores what kind of institution this is: a safety-net nursing and rehabilitation hospital, serving San Francisco’s most medically and economically vulnerable residents (Medi-Cal covers about 95% of its funding), that spent much of TEAM’s own run-up fighting to keep its doors open for reasons entirely unrelated to orthopedic or cardiac surgery.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: What being on the list actually costs it
text:
What being on the list actually costs it
TEAM’s own design limits the practical damage here. The model includes a low-volume policy: a participant with 30 or fewer episodes in a given surgical category over the three-year baseline period faces no downside financial risk in that category for the corresponding performance year, though it can still receive a reconciliation payment if it happens to come in under target. Given that CMS’s own quality data shows zero qualifying postoperative-surgical cases across most of the categories TEAM tracks, Laguna Honda Hospital & Rehabilitation Center likely has at or near zero episodes in every one of the five bundles — which means it is formally a mandatory participant with, in practice, nothing to reconcile. CMS has also said TEAM adds no separate reporting burden beyond a hospital’s existing quality-reporting programs, so the compliance cost of being on the list, for a hospital that runs no relevant episodes, is close to nothing.
That’s the actual shape of the story: not a hospital being squeezed by a payment model it can’t handle, but a hospital carried on a mandatory list built for a kind of care it stopped meaningfully providing, kept there by a licensing category nobody revisited when the selection rule was written.

title: Why Is a Nursing Home With No Operating Room on Medicare’s Mandatory Surgery List?
section: What isn’t established here
text:
What isn’t established here
CMS’s quality-measure footnotes (“no cases met the criteria for this measure”) are strong evidence of zero or near-zero surgical volume in the categories they cover, but they are not the same as a CMS statement of Laguna Honda’s actual TEAM episode count, which CMS has not published. Whether Laguna Honda is one of a kind or one of several former-acute-care CCNs swept into TEAM the same way is untested — it would take a full facility-type check against every one of the 720 hospitals on the roster, which this piece did not do. And nothing here says CMS is unaware of the mismatch; it may simply consider a near-zero-impact mandatory listing not worth an exception process.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
text:
Newsletter




The country’s largest hospital market almost entirely sat out Medicare’s newest mandatory payment program. The reason isn’t policy, and it isn’t politics. It’s a lottery.


Rainfall Health · September 2026
Medicare launched a new payment program in January called the Transforming Episode Accountability Model. Hospitals in it are required to be in it. There is no application and no opting out, and it runs for five years.
The program pulled in 720 hospitals across 45 states. 107 of them are in California, more than any other state. Those California hospitals sit in eleven metropolitan areas. The San Francisco Bay Area has 37. The Inland Empire has 30. San Diego has 15.
Los Angeles has one.
Not one per hospital system, and not one per county. One hospital, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, in a metropolitan area of roughly thirteen million people with more than a hundred acute-care hospitals. And here is the part that makes it strange rather than merely lopsided: Cedars-Sinai is not there because Medicare required it. It volunteered.
So Los Angeles is not just underrepresented in the program. It was left out of it, and the single Los Angeles hospital on the roster is there because it raised its hand.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: First, what the program actually does
text:
First, what the program actually does
Understanding why the omission matters requires a short detour into what hospitals are being signed up for.
Traditionally Medicare pays for surgery in pieces. The operation is one bill. The hospital stay is another. If the patient then spends two weeks in a nursing facility, gets home-health visits, and turns up in the emergency room three weeks later, each of those is billed and paid separately, by whoever provided it. No single organization is on the hook for the total.
This program collapses that. For five kinds of surgery — hip and knee replacement, spinal fusion, heart bypass, surgical repair of a broken hip, and major bowel surgery — the hospital becomes financially accountable for everything that happens to the patient for thirty days after the operation. If the total runs above what Medicare expected, the hospital pays some of the difference back. If it comes in under, the hospital keeps some of the savings. Care that used to be somebody else’s cost is now the hospital’s problem.
That is a significant change in how a hospital has to think, and it is not optional for the hospitals selected. Which is what makes the absence of the nation’s second-largest metropolitan area worth explaining.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The three explanations that don’t hold up
text:
The three explanations that don’t hold up
The intuitive answers all fail, and it is worth watching them fail, because the real answer is not obvious until they do.
It isn’t size. If Medicare had picked the places with the most hospitals or the most Medicare patients, Los Angeles would be at the top of the list rather than absent from it. The Bay Area, with roughly half the population, has 37 participating hospitals.
It isn’t performance. Nothing in the selection process measured how good or bad a hospital is. Quality scores affect what participating hospitals are eventually paid, but they played no part in deciding which hospitals participate. A market cannot be excluded for being too good, and it cannot be excluded for being too bad.
It isn’t politics. The selection was made by formula and published in a federal rule well before anyone knew which hospitals would be affected. There was no list of exemptions to lobby your way onto.
Each of these assumes that somebody looked at Los Angeles and made a decision about it. Nobody did.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: Medicare drew the map at random
text:
Medicare drew the map at random
Here is the mechanism, and it is genuinely surprising for a program that is compulsory: Medicare did not choose the cities. It sampled them.
The federal government divides the country into metropolitan and micropolitan areas — roughly, a population center plus the surrounding counties that commute into it. For this program, 803 of them were eligible. Medicare selected 188, about 23 percent, using what statisticians call stratified random sampling.
Stratified means the areas were first sorted into groups with similar characteristics. Random means that within each group, the selection was a draw. Depending on which group an area landed in, its chance of being picked ran somewhere between 20 and 50 percent.
Los Angeles was eligible. Los Angeles was not drawn.
That is the whole answer, and it is worth sitting with how unusual it is. A mandatory federal payment program, one that will govern how hospitals are paid for five years and reaches 720 of them, has a geographic footprint that was settled by a weighted coin flip.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: What moved the odds
text:
What moved the odds
The grouping was not arbitrary, even if the final draw was. Areas were sorted using four characteristics: how much Medicare had historically spent per surgical episode there, how many hospitals the area contained, how many of those were safety-net hospitals serving large low-income populations, and how much exposure the area had already had to Medicare’s earlier experiments in this style of payment.
That last one matters for Los Angeles.
Medicare has run this kind of program before. From 2016 through the end of 2024 it operated a mandatory bundled-payment model for hip and knee replacement, and Los Angeles was in it — one of only three California metro areas required to participate. In 2018, when Medicare allowed hospitals in most of those markets to withdraw, Los Angeles was in the group that had to stay, because it was among the 34 markets with the highest episode spending in the country.
So by the time the new program was being designed, Los Angeles hospitals had spent nine consecutive years under mandatory bundled payments. And Medicare had decided, deliberately, to weight this round toward places that had not been through that — oversampling areas with little prior exposure, and areas with more safety-net hospitals, on the reasoning that the point of a test is to learn something new.
Nine years of prior participation put Los Angeles in a group with lower odds. Then the draw came up against it.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The proof that it’s chance, not a rule
text:
The proof that it’s chance, not a rule
It would be easy to stop here and conclude Los Angeles was screened out for having already served its time. That’s not quite right, and the correction runs the opposite direction from what it looks like at first.
San Francisco–Oakland went through the same CJR lottery Los Angeles did, but not the same nine years. When Medicare narrowed CJR’s mandatory list to the 34 highest-spending markets in 2018, Los Angeles stayed in. San Francisco didn’t — CMS’s own hospital-list records show it drop from 35 mandatory hospitals before that cut to zero by CJR’s final year. San Francisco’s mandatory exposure ended in 2018. Los Angeles’ ran nine years straight through.
So when TEAM’s own, separate lottery ran, San Francisco actually carried less recent mandatory-bundle history than Los Angeles — and it was drawn anyway, with 37 hospitals, mandatorily, the largest single market in the state. That isn’t a counterexample to the “less exposure, better odds” logic from the last section. It’s that logic landing exactly where it predicted.
The real evidence that Los Angeles’ absence wasn’t a rule comes from a wider look, not a single comparison. Of the 34 markets CJR kept mandatory in 2018 — the tier Los Angeles was in — roughly a third landed on TEAM’s mandatory list anyway, despite carrying the same kind of high prior exposure. High exposure lowered the odds. It didn’t zero them out. Los Angeles was in the majority that didn’t land, not because the outcome was fixed against markets like it, but because a low-probability outcome still happens, just less often than a high-probability one. (A companion piece works through the full 67-market picture, San Francisco and Los Angeles both included: San Francisco Got Let Off the Hook Under CJR. Under TEAM, It Became California’s Biggest Market.)
Which leaves the honest version of the answer. Los Angeles was in a lower-probability group, and it landed on the side of that probability that doesn’t make the roster. There is no policy judgment underneath it to appeal or object to — the two largest hospital markets in California went opposite directions because they were sitting in different odds to begin with, and the draw did what draws do.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The hospital that signed up anyway
text:
The hospital that signed up anyway
Which brings us back to Cedars-Sinai.
Medicare allowed a small number of hospitals outside the selected areas to join voluntarily. Ten nationwide did. Exactly one of them is in California, and it is the one Los Angeles hospital on the roster.
That path had its own rule, and the rule matters here. Federal regulation allowed a hospital to opt in only if two things were both true: its metro area had to be outside the mandatory list, and the hospital had to have already been running a mandatory bundle of its own — either CJR through its last day, December 31, 2024, or BPCI Advanced through December 31, 2025. Cedars-Sinai satisfied both. Its metro area was never drawn, and its nine years in CJR carried straight through to the deadline. The opt-in path exists specifically for a hospital in exactly that position.
It is worth being precise about what that means. Every other California hospital in this program was told to be there. Cedars-Sinai looked at a five-year commitment to absorb financial risk for a month of care after major surgery, in a market where no competitor was under the same obligation, and chose it.
Scale the stakes for a moment. Los Angeles County has more Medicare beneficiaries than any other county in the country — 1.7 million people, in the most recent federal count, nearly double the next-highest county. For the purposes of this specific program, all of that runs through one hospital’s participation.
There are reasonable readings of that decision. A hospital with nine years of bundled-payment experience already has the discharge planning, the post-acute relationships, and the cost data the model rewards, so the marginal cost of participating is low and the potential upside is real. There is also a strategic reading: the skills this program demands are ones Medicare has signaled it will require everywhere soon enough, and building them under a program you chose is easier than building them under one imposed on you.
There’s no public record of how CJR specifically performed for Cedars-Sinai — Medicare doesn’t publish hospital-level results under that program, and the hospital hasn’t said. What is on the record is a different bundle: Cedars-Sinai has run its own orthopedic program under BPCI Advanced, a related but separate Medicare model, since January 2021, and has said publicly that it moved that program from a penalty to a bonus. That isn’t evidence about CJR, and it isn’t a stated reason for the TEAM decision — but it does mean the hospital had recent, direct, and by its own account successful experience with exactly the kind of financial structure TEAM asks for, on top of nine years spent living under CJR’s version of the same idea.

title: Why Does Los Angeles Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: Los Angeles didn’t escape. It got deferred.
text:
Los Angeles didn’t escape. It got deferred.
The last point is the one that matters most for anyone running a hospital in a market that was skipped, and it undercuts any sense of relief.
Medicare has already finalized a second mandatory bundled-payment program, this one specifically for joint replacement, starting January 1, 2028. It is nationwide. It covers essentially every acute-care hospital in the country that is not already in the current program — which is to say, it is aimed squarely at the markets the lottery passed over.
The timing is worth laying out plainly, because it rules out one explanation before anyone raises it. Cedars-Sinai’s CJR run ended December 31, 2024. The TEAM voluntary election window opened the next day and closed January 31, 2025. The program that will eventually reach the hospitals TEAM’s lottery skipped was not proposed until April 14, 2026, and wasn’t finalized until that July. When Cedars-Sinai signed on to TEAM, that program did not exist yet, not even as a draft.
Its episode window is 90 days, not 30.
So the practical result of Los Angeles losing the draw is not exemption. It is a two-year delay, followed by enrollment in a program with an accountability window three times longer. Hospitals in the Bay Area will spend those two years learning to manage a 30-day window. Hospitals in Los Angeles will start in 2028 on a 90-day one.
The one Los Angeles hospital that volunteered is exempt from the 2028 program, because participation in the current one excludes you from it.
Put all of it together and the shape of the case is unusual, not sinister. A stratified lottery left Los Angeles off the mandatory list. A narrow eligibility rule, built around metro-area status and prior bundled-payment history, is what let one hospital back onto the roster anyway. That hospital has recent, documented experience turning a comparable bundle profitable — though not this one, and not for this reason. And the program it might otherwise look like it was avoiding did not exist yet when it signed the paperwork. What’s left is a single hospital carrying the entire program’s footprint for the country’s largest Medicare-enrollment county and its second-largest metro area — an outcome nobody designed, that one hospital chose to be part of anyway.

title: The Thief Who Ran a Company Without Ever Naming It One
text:
Newsletter




For twenty years, Adam Worth was the most wanted man in Europe and almost nobody knew his real name. What he actually built, underneath the theft, was a business.


Rainfall Health · A note for the team · September 2026
On the night of May 25, 1876, a man climbed through a window at 7 Grosvenor Square in London and cut a canvas from its frame with a small knife. It was Thomas Gainsborough’s portrait of Georgiana Cavendish, Duchess of Devonshire — at the time, the most expensive painting in the world. The thief did not sell it. He did not ransom it, not for years. He had it fitted into a custom trunk lined with unbleached cotton, and for the next quarter-century he carried the Duchess with him from city to city, sleeping near her, by most accounts genuinely in love with the painting, long after any sane criminal would have cut his losses. Scotland Yard never caught him for it. When the painting finally reappeared, in 1901, it was because he handed it back himself, on his own terms, for a fraction of what it was worth, no questions asked.
The man’s name was Adam Worth, and by then Scotland Yard had a title for him: the Napoleon of the Criminal World. Arthur Conan Doyle liked the phrase enough to give it to Professor Moriarty outright. Worth never approved of the comparison — Moriarty was violent, and Worth, whatever else he was, was not — but the parallel stuck for a reason. What Worth ran for two decades out of London wasn’t really a gang. Historians who’ve since gone through the Pinkerton archives call it something closer to the first modern criminal corporation. And the strange thing about that description is how much of it holds up once you take the crime part out.

title: The Thief Who Ran a Company Without Ever Naming It One
section: Built like a company, not a gang
text:
Built like a company, not a gang
He was born in Prussia in 1844 and raised in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the son of an honest, unremarkable, hardworking family — the quiet kid, good at math, no trouble in school. At seventeen he lied about his age to enlist in the Union Army, then deserted, then re-enlisted under a fake name, then deserted again, then got mistakenly recorded as killed at the Second Battle of Bull Run. On the government’s books, Adam Worth died before he turned twenty. He decided to treat that as an opportunity rather than a problem. A dead man can’t be drafted, and a dead man doesn’t have to be anyone in particular.
He drifted into New York’s pickpocket gangs and came to the attention of Fredericka “Marm” Mandelbaum, who ran the largest fencing operation in the country and had an eye for talent. Her read on him, relayed secondhand through everyone who worked with him afterward, was consistent: calm under pressure, not a drinker, not a brawler, methodical to the point of being boring — and for that specific line of work, boring was the highest compliment available. She started giving him responsibilities she didn’t usually hand to newcomers. He teamed up with a safecracker who went by Piano Charlie Bullard — genuinely gifted at the piano, which is how he got the name, and which also happened to be a convenient excuse to be in a saloon scouting a target. In 1869 the two of them tunneled into Boston’s Boylston National Bank, one of the first professionally engineered bank burglaries in American history, and put themselves permanently on the Pinkerton Agency’s books.

He believed a man with brains had no need for a gun. There was always a way — a better way — worked out ahead of time.
— William Pinkerton, on Worth’s operating philosophy

That line is the whole operation in miniature. Worth genuinely believed violence was bad math, not bad ethics. A gun turns a quiet theft into a headline, and a headline turns a headline into police pressure, and police pressure is the one thing patience can’t outwait. So he banned weapons outright — anyone in his crew who carried one was gone, no matter how good they were — and what that bought him was a two-decade run with almost no arrests and almost no public attention, at a moment when everyone doing this kind of work was getting caught constantly. Victorian police, in what reads like grudging admiration, called him the most patient burglar on record.
By the London years he wasn’t managing a crew, he was managing an org chart. Separate teams for safecracking, forgery, jewelry work, surveillance — each with its own expertise, each reporting up through him. Stolen goods never got sold anywhere near where they were stolen; a diamond lifted in London would pass through brokers in Antwerp and Hamburg and New York before it ever surfaced for sale, somewhere like Cape Town, far enough from the original crime that no local detective had any reason to connect the two. He financed the whole thing partly through real import-export businesses, which gave the money somewhere legitimate to sit. And he paid people promptly, funded their legal defense when they got caught, and looked after their families while they served time — which, in a line of work built almost entirely on people who could disappear with your money and never look back, bought him a loyalty that read, to more than one contemporary, as almost mafia-grade.

title: The Thief Who Ran a Company Without Ever Naming It One
section: What actually transfers
text:
What actually transfers
None of this requires admiring the man. It requires noticing that he worked out, well before most legitimate businesses did, that discretion is a structural advantage rather than a personality trait — that the boring move is usually the correct one, that a team of specialists beats a crew of generalists, that people stay loyal to whoever actually pays them and shows up for them when things go wrong. A health-tech startup doesn’t need the fencing network. It needs the underlying logic: don’t take the loud, aggressive shortcut on anything compliance- or clinical-adjacent, because the scrutiny it invites always costs more than the time it saves. Don’t let one partner, one integration, one client be a single point of failure, the way Worth refused to run everything through one broker. Keep the follow-through on internal commitments consistent enough that people trust it, because that’s the actual retention lever, not the perks sitting on top of it. And when the work touches anything regulatory or clinical, take the slow, correct route rather than the fast, reversible one — the same instinct that got Worth called the most patient burglar on record is just measure twice, cut once, with better tailoring.
There’s one more piece of his operation worth naming without chasing it very far. Worth compartmentalized everything — separate cells for each specialty, deliberately kept in the dark about each other, so that if one person got arrested, they couldn’t hand the whole network to the police. It’s a genuinely interesting idea, and it’s not actually a foreign one in healthcare: it’s close to the logic already sitting underneath HIPAA’s minimum-necessary standard and ordinary least-privilege access control. Worth a five-minute conversation about who has access to what, and no further than that — the version of this that isolates teams from each other rather than just isolating data is a liability wearing an efficiency’s clothes.

title: The Thief Who Ran a Company Without Ever Naming It One
section: Where the story stops being useful
text:
Where the story stops being useful
It’s worth being honest about where the story stops being useful, too. Worth’s thirty-year run worked specifically because Victorian policing was fragmented, cross-border cooperation barely existed, and forensic science hadn’t been invented yet. That gap is the entire reason Interpol exists now — it’s the direct institutional answer to the kind of exploit his career depended on. Nobody operating a health company today gets to work in the world he had; they work in the one built specifically to close it. His family, meanwhile, had no idea what he actually did — his wife and children believed, for their entire lives with him, that he simply traveled a great deal for trade. That isn’t a management technique. It’s the definition of a conflict of interest that no real business, let alone a healthcare one, gets to run.
And for all of it — the crews, the network, the loyalty, the two decades nobody could touch him — Adam Worth died in London in 1902, broke, and was buried under a false name in Highgate Cemetery, a short walk from Karl Marx. The “corporation” label is a compliment historians paid him afterward, looking back at the structure. It was never something he’d have called a going concern while he was building it. That’s the part worth remembering before borrowing too much from the model: the parts that worked, worked. The whole thing still wasn’t built to last, and it didn’t.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
text:
Newsletter




San Francisco and Modesto both lost mandatory CJR status in 2018 and kept running the program voluntarily through its final day — the same trajectory, right up to TEAM’s own separate lottery. San Francisco drew 37 hospitals, mandatorily. Modesto drew none, not even a single voluntary joiner.


Rainfall Health · September 2026
Los Angeles has one hospital in Medicare’s TEAM model, and it’s there because it volunteered. San Francisco has 37, the most of any market in California, and every one of them is mandatory. Modesto has zero — not mandatory, not voluntary, none.
Los Angeles’ history is different from the other two. It was one of only 34 markets CMS kept mandatory in an older joint-replacement bundle, CJR, when the program narrowed its list in 2018 — staying in for all nine years of CJR’s run, 2016 through 2024. San Francisco and Modesto share a different history: both were downgraded out of mandatory status in that same 2018 cut, and both kept running CJR voluntarily through the program’s final day. Same drop, same continuation, the identical nine years in some form. One of them is now the largest TEAM market in California. The other has nothing.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
section: What TEAM asks of a hospital
text:
What TEAM asks of a hospital
TEAM, the Transforming Episode Accountability Model, is a five-year Medicare program that makes a hospital financially responsible for the cost and outcomes of a patient’s care for 30 days after five kinds of surgery: lower-extremity joint replacement, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass grafting, surgical hip and femur fracture treatment, and major bowel procedures. 720 hospitals are on the mandatory roster nationwide, selected not by application but by geography: any hospital paid under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System with a CMS Certification Number address inside one of 188 metropolitan or micropolitan areas CMS drew by stratified random sample, out of roughly 803 eligible areas, is in. Outside those 188 areas, a narrow voluntary pathway lets a small number of additional hospitals opt in anyway, if they ran a mandatory bundle of their own — CJR through December 31, 2024, or BPCI Advanced through December 31, 2025. 10 hospitals did, nationwide.
Three California markets ran CJR for nine years, in different mixes of mandatory and voluntary status. Their outcomes on TEAM’s separate, later lottery could not be more different.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
section: Three markets, one history, three outcomes
text:
Three markets, one history, three outcomes
California had three MSAs in CJR’s original 2016 mandatory lottery: Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward (renamed San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont under the current OMB delineation), and Modesto. All three ran under mandatory CJR from 2016 through 2018. In 2018, CMS cut mandatory CJR participation to the 34 markets with the highest historical episode spending; Los Angeles’ spending was high enough to stay in, while San Francisco and Modesto dropped to CJR’s voluntary-continuation tier. All three, including the two that dropped tiers, kept running CJR episodes through the model’s final day, December 31, 2024 — a hospital only needed to have run the model at some point through that date to qualify later for TEAM’s voluntary opt-in, and CJR’s own hospital-list spreadsheets show hospitals in all three markets doing exactly that.
Then TEAM ran its own, unrelated stratified draw in 2024, and the three markets split three ways:

Los Angeles’ one hospital, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (CCN 050625), is there because it used the voluntary opt-in built for hospitals with prior mandatory-bundle history. San Francisco’s 37 are there because CMS’s 2024 draw happened to select that CBSA outright, mandatorily, for reasons unrelated to its CJR history. Modesto’s CBSA wasn’t drawn, and unlike Los Angeles, no hospital inside it used the voluntary pathway to join anyway. Every plausible route onto TEAM’s roster came up empty for a market that ran the same nine-year CJR program as the other two, under the same voluntary-continuation status San Francisco also carried after 2018.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
section: Confirming the zero
text:
Confirming the zero
This finding rests on checking every row of CMS’s own roster, not just the mandatory ones. CMS’s TEAM Participant List — the same file this article’s other figures are computed from, and the same file CMS republishes quarterly — carries 720 hospitals total, mandatory and voluntary combined. None of them list a CBSA of Modesto, CA (CBSA code 33700). A fresh pull of that same file directly from CMS’s website, dated August 18, 2026 and carrying 722 hospitals (two more than the October 6, 2026 vendored copy this article otherwise uses, which is dated April 15, 2026 and carries 720), shows the identical result: zero Modesto rows, and the same one-hospital Los Angeles and 37-hospital San Francisco counts. The finding isn’t an artifact of a stale file.
It also isn’t an artifact of Modesto having no hospitals to send. CMS’s Hospital General Information file — pulled fresh from CMS’s provider-data API for this article — lists five acute-care hospitals in Stanislaus County, the single county that makes up the Modesto CBSA: Doctors Medical Center and Memorial Medical Center in Modesto, Stanislaus Surgical Hospital in Modesto, Emanuel Medical Center in Turlock, and Oak Valley Hospital District in Oakdale. None of the five appears anywhere on TEAM’s participant list, mandatory or voluntary.
The voluntary pathway specifically requires prior CJR or BPCI Advanced history through the program’s own final performance year. None of the five Stanislaus County hospitals shows up in CMS’s Model Year 7 BPCI Advanced participant list either — the roster covering the model’s last performance period, which ran through December 31, 2025. So the gap isn’t that a Modesto hospital was eligible to volunteer and chose not to. On the record CMS has published, no hospital in Modesto’s CBSA had a BPCI Advanced pathway available to it at all, and the one pathway that was available — CJR history — went unused.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
section: Why markets with the same history landed differently
text:
Why markets with the same history landed differently
TEAM’s selection wasn’t blind to CJR history. CMS’s own final rule sorted every eligible CBSA into a stratum based on the median of four factors: average historical episode spending, the number of IPPS-paid acute-care hospitals in the area, the number of safety-net hospitals with qualifying episode volume, and — the factor that matters here — past exposure to CMS’s own bundled-payment models, including CJR and BPCI Advanced, between October 2013 and December 2022. CMS said explicitly, in the rule proposing this design, that it intended to oversample CBSAs with low past bundled-payment exposure, while still giving some high-exposure CBSAs a chance of selection rather than excluding them outright. A market with nine years of CJR participation — mandatory the whole way, like Los Angeles, or mandatory at first and voluntary after 2018, like San Francisco and Modesto — would plausibly land in the higher-exposure stratum CMS deliberately gave lower draw odds, not zero odds: San Francisco proves the higher-exposure stratum can still be drawn, but at lower odds than a market with no bundled-payment history at all.
That mechanism explains the general pattern already documented elsewhere in this research: former-mandatory CJR markets nationwide were selected into TEAM at 35.3%, well above the roughly 23.5 percent national baseline rate for all eligible CBSAs, metro and micro combined. Former-voluntary-tier markets — San Francisco and Modesto’s own group — landed close to that baseline, at 21.2%. It does not explain why San Francisco drew and Modesto didn’t, despite sharing the identical voluntary-tier history; that’s the ordinary variance of a probabilistic draw, and CMS has not published, and this article did not independently reconstruct, the exact selection probability assigned to Modesto’s specific stratum.
Size is the more concrete difference. Stanislaus County’s five acute-care hospitals are a small fraction of the hospital count in Los Angeles or San Francisco’s much larger CBSAs, and the number of IPPS-paid hospitals in a CBSA is itself one of CMS’s four stratification factors. Modesto’s metro population is about 557,000, roughly a fortieth of Los Angeles’ and a tenth of San Francisco’s-Oakland’s, and smaller than any of the three biggest one-hospital-TEAM markets this research has already covered elsewhere (Los Angeles, Miami, and Tampa, whose metro Medicare-enrollment footprints run from roughly 770,000 up to 2.3 million). A market this size sits far more plausibly in whatever “low” bucket several of TEAM’s four stratification factors define than a market the size of Los Angeles or San Francisco does — a plausible contributor to lower selection odds, though not one this article can isolate cleanly from the past-exposure factor above, since CMS classifies CBSAs on all four factors jointly rather than one at a time.

title: Modesto and San Francisco Had the Same CJR History. One Got 37 TEAM Hospitals. The Other Got Zero.
section: What isn’t established here
text:
What isn’t established here
CMS has not published a hospital-by-hospital reconstruction of exactly which selection probability Modesto’s CBSA carried, so this article cannot say precisely how unlikely a zero outcome was, only that it fits a documented, deliberate oversampling design rather than an obvious error. The 2018 cut of CJR’s original 67 mandatory MSAs down to 34 is independently well documented for Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Modesto specifically, but the full 34-MSA list is this research bank’s own reconstruction, built by reapplying CMS’s stated criterion to CMS’s own historical payment data, not a verbatim CMS-published table — see this project’s prior published article on the broader 67-market pattern for that caveat in full. And nothing here should be read as CMS being unaware of, or having erred regarding, Modesto’s absence from TEAM; a stratified random draw is expected to produce outcomes like this one for some markets, by design.


About the data. Hospital and roster figures in this article are computed at render time from the TEAM Participant List - 2026Q2 (as of April 15, 2026), the same file Medicare publishes as the official TEAM participant roster. A fresh pull of that file directly from CMS, retrieved September 23, 2026 and dated August 18, 2026 (722 hospitals, versus the vendored copy’s 720), was checked against it and produced the same Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Modesto figures; both are cited below. CMS Hospital General Information and BPCI Advanced participant-list figures were pulled directly from CMS’s provider-data API and cms.gov, respectively, and archived alongside this project’s research files. Built October 6, 2026.
Disclaimer. Rainfall Health is not a hospital, health system, or health care provider. This article is prepared by health care industry professionals, not clinicians, and does not constitute clinical, legal, financial, or regulatory advice. It does not assess, rate, or make claims about the quality of care provided by any individual hospital or organization, and it does not allege that CMS did anything improper — a stratified random draw producing a zero result for one market is an expected outcome of the method CMS itself published, not evidence of an error.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
text:
Newsletter




Three of the country’s biggest, most recognizable hospital markets came up almost empty in Medicare’s newest mandatory payment program. In every case, the same kind of hospital volunteered to fill the gap.


Rainfall Health · September 2026
Los Angeles has one hospital in Medicare’s newest mandatory payment program. That fact alone is strange enough to write about — it’s the country’s second-largest metro area, and it’s represented by a single hospital that didn’t even have to be there.
It turns out Los Angeles isn’t alone in being alone. Miami has exactly one hospital in the same program. So does Tampa. All three are among the biggest, best-known hospital markets in the country. All three came up with a single participant. And in all three cases, that one hospital is there because it volunteered, not because Medicare required it.
Three cities, three near-total absences, three volunteers. That’s not a coincidence anymore. It’s a pattern, and the pattern has a specific, traceable cause.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: What the program asks of a hospital
text:
What the program asks of a hospital
The program is the Transforming Episode Accountability Model, TEAM for short. It’s a five-year Medicare initiative that makes a hospital financially responsible for everything that happens to a patient for thirty days after five kinds of surgery — hip and knee replacement, spinal fusion, heart bypass, hip fracture repair, and major bowel surgery. Spend more than Medicare expected across that window, or have the patient come back in, and the hospital’s number moves. It is mandatory for the hospitals selected, and there is no opting out once selected.
720 hospitals were selected this way. None of them applied. Medicare simply divided the country into metropolitan and micropolitan areas and drew 188 of roughly 803 eligible ones, using stratified random sampling weighted by a handful of characteristics. Every hospital sitting inside a drawn area was in. Every hospital outside one wasn’t, with one narrow exception: a small number of hospitals outside the selected areas were allowed to join anyway, if they qualified. Ten did, nationwide.
Three of those ten volunteers are the one-hospital cities this piece is about.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The same shape, three times
text:
The same shape, three times
Cedars-Sinai Medical Center represents all of Los Angeles. Keralty Hospital represents all of Miami. Morton Plant Hospital represents all of Tampa. Each metro area has dozens of acute-care hospitals. Each has exactly one on the TEAM roster, and in each case it’s the same story: the metro’s area wasn’t drawn into the mandatory list, and one hospital opted in through the program’s narrow voluntary pathway.
That pathway has a specific eligibility rule, and it’s the same rule behind all three cases. A hospital can volunteer only if its metro area is outside the mandatory list, and only if it already ran a mandatory bundle of its own — either the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement model, CJR, through its last day, December 31, 2024, or a related program called BPCI Advanced through December 31, 2025. All three hospitals here qualify on the CJR side.
This is where the pattern gets harder to wave off as chance. CMS’s own CJR hospital-list spreadsheets, cross-checked directly rather than taken from a summary, show all three hospitals were mandatory CJR participants for years, right up to the program’s final months. Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (CCN 050625) is on both the pre-2018 list and CMS’s July 2024 list — nine straight years. Morton Plant Hospital (CCN 100127) is on both. Keralty Hospital (CCN 100284) is on both too, though it shows up under a different name on the earlier one: it was Westchester General Hospital before the Keralty Group acquired it in 2020.
So all three were mandatory CJR hospitals for essentially the program’s entire run, in metro areas that CMS’s 2018 restructuring specifically kept mandatory — the tier reserved for the markets with the highest historical episode spending in the country. Then, when TEAM’s lottery drew its 188 areas, none of these three metros came up. And in every one of the three, a hospital that had just spent nine years under one mandatory bundle used the narrow window CMS left open to step into the next one, voluntarily, while the market around it sat out.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The scale of what one hospital is standing in for
text:
The scale of what one hospital is standing in for
It’s worth being precise about how much ground a single hospital is covering in each case, because the three cities aren’t the same size.
Los Angeles is the second-largest metro area in the country, behind only New York. Miami is sixth-largest, ahead of Atlanta and Washington, D.C. Tampa is seventeenth. Measured by Medicare enrollment across the counties each metro area covers, Los Angeles’ footprint runs to roughly 2.3 million beneficiaries, Miami’s to about 1.3 million, and Tampa’s to about 770,000. Three very different scales, and in every one of them, TEAM’s entire footprint is a single hospital’s participation.
That’s the part that makes this more than a quirky coincidence. A lottery that happens to skip one huge market is a story. A lottery that skips three of the country’s biggest markets, in a way that traces back to the exact same eligibility mechanism each time, is a pattern in how the selection interacts with prior bundled-payment history — even though nothing about the draw itself targeted these cities by name.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: No hospital has said why
text:
No hospital has said why
None of the three has published anything explaining the decision. Medicare doesn’t release hospital-level results from CJR, and none of Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Morton Plant Hospital, or Keralty Hospital has said publicly why it chose to keep going under a new program the moment the old one ended. That’s true across all three cases, not just one, which suggests the honest answer isn’t a hospital-specific secret. It’s a structural one: nine years of running discharge planning and cost tracking under a mandatory bundle leaves a hospital with the infrastructure to do it again cheaply, whatever the individual reasoning was.

title: Why Do Miami, Tampa, and Los Angeles Each Have Only One Hospital in Medicare’s TEAM Model?
section: The one that got them all excluded is coming for them anyway
text:
The one that got them all excluded is coming for them anyway
None of the three markets actually escaped anything. Medicare has already finalized a second mandatory bundled-payment program, this one specifically for joint replacement, starting January 1, 2028, nationwide, on a 90-day window instead of 30. It reaches essentially every acute-care hospital not already in TEAM — which is precisely the hospitals in Los Angeles, Miami, and Tampa that the lottery passed over the first time.
The three volunteers are exempt from that program, because participating in TEAM already excludes a hospital from it. So the practical effect of all three lottery misses is the same: a two-year deferral, then a landing in a longer, harder version of the same idea, for every hospital in these three markets except the one that already opted into the shorter one.
Put the pieces together and none of it reads as coincidence. A stratified lottery skipped three of the biggest hospital markets in the country. All three had spent nine years under the same prior mandatory program, in the tier CMS had deliberately weighted away from resampling. In every one, a single hospital used the same narrow rule to opt back in anyway, without explaining why. And in every one, the market it stepped in for is now deferred, not exempt, from a longer program arriving in 2028. Three cities, one mechanism, working exactly the way it was built to work — just not the way most people would guess from the outside.
